#1413. Man United are a rotten, shambolic mess. They lack intelligence, look uncoached and fumbling, failing Michael Carrick is not the man to arrest this trauma, writes IAN LADYMAN

Published: 14:32 EST, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 20:25 EST, 8 November 2026

Manchester United do not have a football team, more a collection of adrenaline junkies. Over time, it will not be enough.

So deficient are Michael Carrick's players that they surely can't keep their manager in a job for much longer. For the most part United are shambolic, a mess. At times they play football so devoid of intelligence and competence that it's almost impossible to fathom. They look uncoached.

Yet here they were for the second night running at Old Trafford, completing a lap of honour at full-time while their supporters sang the name of Carrick as he completed his own journey in front of the Stretford End towards the tunnel.

United – it's worth pointing out – are third bottom of the Premier League. They haven't won in the league since August and have conceded more goals across all competitions – 30 – than any team bar Crystal Palace in Europe's top divisions.

But at Old Trafford they will cling to anything to help them look in the mirror without laughing and currently the currency is comebacks. There was one against Roma in the Champions League last Tuesday and here – quite remarkably – there were two in one game.

None of it should really mean anything in the grand scheme. United are rotten, capable of playing effectively only when something gives them an energy spike with which to roll. It makes for quite hypnotic theatre but has inadequacy and desperation at its core.

Patrick Dorgu (centre) scored a late equaliser as troubled Man United drew 4-4 vs Aston Villa

Dorgu scored in the 96th-minute with this header but United sit 18th in the Premier League

Despite the draw, Michael Carrick's position as United head coach looks increasingly doubtful

It won't sustain them or indeed their fumbling, failing manager. But for the moment it's what they have and what they are.

MANCHESTER UNITED (4-2-3-1): Lammens 4; Mazraoui 4, Yoro 6, Maguire 5 (Heaven 46, 5), Dalot 3 (Dorgu 66, 8); Tielemans 6 (Mount 66, 5), Mainoo 6; Amad 5 (Lacey 66, 7), Fernandes 6, Cunha 7; Mbeumo 5 (Zirkzee 83, 7)

Goals: Fernandes (16 pen), Tielemans (44), Zirkzee (90+2), Dorgu (90+6)

ASTON VILLA (4-2-3-1): Suzuki 6; Harwood-Bellis 5, Lindelof 6, Torres 6, Maatsen 4; Goretzka 6 (Mbaye 78, 6), Kamara 4; Alysson 7 (Barkley 71, 6), McGinn 8 (Hemmings 71, 6), Manzambi 6; Jackson 6 (Madjo 86)

Goals: Alysson (1), Jackson (4), McGinn (48 pen), Goretzka (53)

Here, they twice trailed by two, at the start of both halves. They were 2-0 down after only four minutes and 4-2 behind after 53. Somehow they managed not to lose.

The two goals United scored in added time at the end of the game came from absolutely nowhere. On the touchline Carrick – free from total humiliation for the second time in six days – raised a single finger to the sky.

In the directors' box – where the TV companies seem to have a camera permanently trained these days – fist pumps were in evidence from those in United blazers.

This was another uncomfortable afternoon for Messrs Ratcliffe, Wilcox and Berrada. A collection of new banners in the crowd made feelings known.

For now, Carrick is being spared any of the blame. That is strange and wrong but tells us much about the confused nature of the modern United. If they blame one of their own then they really do have nowhere left to go in search of self-respect.

United's opening against Roma last week had been traumatic enough. This was even worse but the root of it was desperately familiar – incompetent football.

The hapless United full-back Diogo Dalot was to blame for the first goal as Villa's Brazilian Alysson blasted his shot through the Portuguese's limp challenge. Later – after conceding a second half penalty – Dalot was booed off by his own fans.

That was painful and unedifying but completely understandable. Dalot has played more than 250 games for United yet has never even been good enough.

Aston Villa took the lead after just 59 seconds when Alysson (centre) scored at Old Trafford

Nicolas Jackson (centre) doubled the visitors' lead on four minutes as they made a dream start

Bruno Fernandes pulled one back for the hosts with a penalty on 16 minutes in a crazy start

For goal two, goalkeeper Senne Lammens was culpable as he pushed Alysson's shot into the path of Nicolas Jackson.

Once again United were in sink or swim territory. Once again, amazingly, they kept their heads above water – at least for a while.

Boubacar Kamara's 13th minute challenge on Matheus Cunha was stupid as the Brazilian was heading away from goal. But the Bruno Fernandes penalty that followed was calm and precise and the shot of belief United needed was theirs.

For the next 20 minutes or so, Carrick's team played well off the back of it. It was the only part of their game that will look good on the highlights. The United front four pressed and harried the Villa defence to the extent that Unai Emery's team couldn't get up the field.

Villa keeper Zion Suzuki saved well from a Cunha curler while subsequent shots from Fernandes, Kobbie Mainoo and Amad Diallo took deflections and narrowly missed the target.

At some stage it felt as though United's energy must drop. Over time it did. But then they equalised.

Moments after seeing Suzuki save one of his own efforts, Amad found space to pull the ball back for Youri Tielemans who placed his first United goal in from 18 yards against his old club. Carrick's team deserved to be level at that stage and had played some enterprising football to get there. But their self-harm gene surfaced again before long.

Youri Tielemans (right) brought United level before half-time with this strike vs his old club

John McGinn put Villa ahead again just minutes after half-time from the penalty spot

Leon Goretkza (left) made it 4-2 to Villa with this close-range strike as they looked set to win

Joshua Zirkzee (left) pulled one back in second-half stoppage-time with this finish for United

Alysson had almost scored with the last big moment of the first half and in the 47th minute he drew an utterly dumb foul from Dalot and John McGinn scored the penalty firmly.

United are beyond compare in the Premier League when it comes to this kind of thing. Who else in the top flight concedes the kind of goals they do? A case in point came in the 53rd minute.

McGinn's free-kick was heading across goal and away when United defender Leny Yoro inexplicably headed it towards his own goal. Lammens somehow touched the ball on to the bar but when it dropped Leon Goretzka poked it in.

That was the 16th goal United had conceded in the last five games and this time the attempt at a fightback was more muted.

There were some half chances – shots from Cunha and Fernandes – and some territory in which to play.

But this was a game Villa were now able to control rather better and they looked set to ease home until Patrick Dorgu crossed for Joshua Zirkzee to ease a goal in from out of nothing in the 2nd minute of added time.

Old Trafford was emptying fast by the time Dorgu headed in a 96th equaliser from a corner. But by then the collective blood was up once more and it was enough.

Villa appealed for a foul on goalkeeper Suzuki and it's true Lammens had gone looking for him. Was the contact between the two 'keepers significant enough to warrant VAR intervention? Probably not. United had their draw and they had a point.

If the season ended today, they would be down. Yet they were cheered off. Some things you just can't make up.

Thomas O. Auer is in the Department of Biology and at the Food Research and Innovation Center, University of Fribourg, 1700 Fribourg, Switzerland.

When the goddess Hera set out to seduce Zeus in Homer’s The Iliad, she did not start with her looks, but with perfume, preparing an ambrosial oil with a fragrance that filled “heaven and Earth”. The idea that scent kindles desire still captures our imaginations, but how odours act on the human brain to drive sexual attraction is unclear, and decades of searching for sex pheromones have produced no convincing candidates. That is not the case for insects, in which chemical sex signals are well understood. Writing in Nature, Brand et al.1 add another piece to the mosaic of sexual communication. By comparing fly species that are adapted to different host fruits, they show that food odours can be key for male sexual arousal. Flies combine this cue with information about their social environment to get into the mood for mating.

#1411. The cheats prosper: Man City thrash 10-man Liverpool

Just when the Premier League and the world outside of east Manchester and Abu Dhabi needed Liverpool to step up, to strike back, to make a point, they faltered. Maybe it was unfair to expect them to do so, given the circumstances. But unfairness, lack of clarity and uncertainty are all prevailing moods in English football at present.

How we had rubbed our hands in anticipation of Manchester City having to play their first league fixture here at Anfield after being found guilty of industrial-scale fraud with 114 of the 115 financial charges being proven against them.

It felt apt that it was at the home of Liverpool, who, along with Arsenal, possess the strongest sense of grievance at having been denied trophies and glory by City’s cheating. As expected, there were banners everywhere at Anfield. “A generation of supporters cheated,” one read and it summed up the depth of the anger.

Their fans would surely create the kind of bear-pit atmosphere that would leave City in no doubt at the vitriol that will rain down on them from now on. At every away ground. Liverpool could set the tone. The defiance.

This is a team who can stir the blood, surf the emotion and triumph against the odds more than any other; who have a proud history of doing so. Who feel the injustice at its most acute and could feed off that.

In the end Liverpool suffered their first defeat of the season. Their first under Andoni Iraola. And comprehensively so. It could not have come at a worse time for them and for the Premier League, and for the fans of every other club who wanted to see City humbled. On the pitch.

There was another sense of injustice. Up until the dismissal of Ryan Gravenberch, Liverpool were the better side. Especially as they attacked the Kop in the second half, drawing saves from Gianluigi Donnarumma, and began to build the kind of momentum that has, over the years, appeared to suck the ball into the net.

Ryan Gravenberch is OFF 🟥 https://t.co/IVIHNzqw6k

The midfielder’s first yellow card looked harsh. His second, for a foul on substitute Jérémy Doku was less so (but still not clear-cut) and it meant Liverpool had to play the final third of the game with 10 men. Instead of weaponising that; they wilted and the fans directed their frustration at referee Chris Kavanagh, believing he was lenient towards City.

This is not a slight on Iraola, but it is hard to imagine Jürgen Klopp not riding that wave of emotion more effectively and wringing more out of the available players. Turning to the fans; imploring them; cajoling them.

Instead it was City making the statement with an extraordinary power play as they scored three times in 13 minutes, inspired by Doku, whose cameo made him man of the match. That City could hold the winger back, on the bench, only to introduce him with such devastating effect again pointed to their phenomenal strength in depth.

They are again three points clear at the top, with six wins from six games, ahead of champions Arsenal and there is a frightening awesomeness about them at present that will make the Premier League shudder. For several reasons. What if they run away with it this season before being sanctioned, probably sometime in the spring? Where will that leave the competition?

In the face of City’s power and the adversity of losing Gravenberch, Liverpool simply could not cope. They were already depleted – without Dominik Szoboszlai, Alexander Isak, Hugo Ekitike and Cody Gakpo – and needed some of their other big signings to respond.

But this was not a good day for Bradley Barcola or Florian Wirtz, in particular, and it felt telling that the latter was withdrawn soon after Erling Haaland opened the scoring. He could, in fact, have also been sent off after catching Elliot Anderson late. The German’s contribution was once more woefully negligible; worryingly marginal. He was lightweight and so, ultimately, were Liverpool.

Erling Haaland gives Manchester City the lead against Liverpool 🎯 https://t.co/cELo5y60Fk

In fact, Liverpool’s best performers were the young attackers Victor Muñoz and, making his first league start as a makeshift centre-forward, Lewis Koumas, who is just 21. Against that, City unleashed a battery of forward talent.

"Koumas & Munoz were better than the two £100million players!" Jamie Carragher is still disappointed with what he's seeing from Florian Wirtz in a Liverpool shirt 😬🔴 https://t.co/jJwOZbPJ4b

Was it an unfair advantage? It appears City have been thriving off that for some time and, while this team were not signed during the years the club have been found guilty of cheating, the argument is, of course, that they would not have joined without the sporting supremacy.

Certainly not Haaland, despite his avowed love for City. That cannot be doubted as his father, Alf-Inge, a former midfielder for the club, stood celebrating in the away end. The striker missed one chance when he should have scored, sent through on goal, shaking his head in disbelief at getting his angles wrong. It felt like a warning and that went unheeded as Doku, who had replaced one of their big summer signings in Iliman Ndiaye, cut in from the left with his shot deflecting into Haaland’s path. He made no mistake with a powerful, first-time finish.

Doku soon added a second, a sublime strike, as he dribbled goalwards, defenders backing off, and he arced a right-footed shot high beyond Alisson Becker’s grasp.

There were delighted chants of “olé” from the City supporters and that arrogance was rewarded by a strutting, emphatic third goal. It was finished by the mercurial Rayan Cherki after he was sent clear by a backheel from Josko Gvardiol, another substitute.

A moment of individual brilliance from Rayan Cherki to put the game beyond all doubt 🤯 https://t.co/wvmTMZcGhW

It captured City’s swagger, their sense of responding to what they regard as an injustice – that they maintain will be overturned on appeal – the sense they are going to continue to create an almighty headache for the Premier League. In a sea of uncertainty as to what will now happen, that is something we can be sure of.

“Cheats,” loudly boomed around Anfield from the home fans before the PA played Fleetwood Mac’s Tell Me Lies at the final whistle, as the players walked off. Those signs of defiance were not matched on the pitch. Although it may be a song City will get used to hearing for the rest of this extraordinary, unprecedented campaign.

Enzo Maresca hailed Manchester City’s ability to “make our own noise” after their emphatic 3-0 win at Liverpool.

In the first fixture since being found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges laid against them for serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules, City made their statement on the pitch as they re-established a three-point lead at the top of the table.

“It was not easy for the players after the last two, three weeks, but they dealt with it very well,” Maresca, the head coach, said. “I said during the week we need to learn to deal with the outside noise because of the situation, because that will be there. But we have to make our own noise.

“Zero-three at Anfield away is a great result, for sure. I think all the organisation needs a win like this. It’s good for all [of] the club.”

Maresca said City will have to get used to such hostile occasions, with Liverpool fans making clear their anger over the judgment, and added: “All the away games are going to be with noise.”

Maresca confirmed that chief executive Ferran Soriano and director of football Hugo Viana had travelled on the team bus to Anfield in a sign of unity.

“Ferran was there, Hugo was there. We were all together,” Maresca said. “For the importance of the game, Liverpool away, Anfield away. It’s good to be together.”

The Italian claimed that despite the verdict, and the attention and uncertainty as to what will happen next, it had not affected his squad.

“The players just focus on the football. They are not thinking about the future,” he said. “It’s how we learn to deal with the noise. It’s our duty to make noise and to do that we win games. You cannot imagine how happy I am. Hopefully I am going to speak about this situation when we are going to win the appeal.”

The Liverpool boss told BBC MOTD: “I think the first part is that we played two different games. One until the red card, and then after. For 60 minutes, the players were very good. The second game from the red card was where City were better than us.

“The first yellow card was just a kick in the toe. It was nothing. It was a normal foul. It was the moment when we were pushing more. The momentum was coming for us and the atmosphere in the stadium was so nice. We conceded very little in the first half. We did a really good job. The second half, we were translating into chances.

“You learn a lot in games like today. I am very proud of my players. They put the work rate and everything in today. It’s a loss and we didn’t get anything from the performance but I liked it a lot.”

“We really stuck together out there, fought for each other and played well. We’ve shown courage and three points is good. I thought we did really well to quieten the crowd. We struggled in the first half a little bit, but in the second half we were a lot better.”

There is no doubt Enzo Maresca will be the happier head coach. Liverpool, at times, have played some of their best football of the season so far and carried a threat with youngsters Victor Munoz and Lewis Koumas doing well. Even if Andoni Iraola will want more from Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola. Alexis MacAllister has gone closest. But Manchester City have undoubtedly weathered the storm and gradually gained more and more control and shown a greater threat. In saying that it is, in truth, a game that has really yet to fire. A big second-half awaits.

It’s been a cagey encounter here at Anfield and nothing separates these two sides. There’s been a distinct lack of chances and attacking quality, with the defences prevailing.

There will be one minute of added time to round off this first half. Can either side find the first goal before the break?

Alisson does well to parry away Anderson’s fizzing cross at the near post. Liverpool then hack it clear. After an initial spell of Liverpool pressure in the opening 20 minutes, City have grown into the contest and look like the more confident side.

Donnarumma is a picture of calmness as he manoeuvres away from Munoz with a delightful touch and turn.

Anderson beats Wirtz to the ball, fashioning an opening for Cherki. The mercurial playmaker cuts inside and tries to bend a shot for the far corner, but he can’t wrap his foot around the strike as it flys way off target and out for a throw-in.

A small point to make, in amongst everything else, but Liverpool have recruited a jewel in Jeremy Jacquet. He is going to take care of Erling Haaland at every opportunity and this is the battle that will have so much of a bearing on the contest. Haaland only needs a second to make a difference - Jacquet cannot switch off at any stage.

Fernandez’s whipped, dipping strike from outside the box is caught by Alisson. That is City’s first shot of the game.

Will Liverpool regret not capitalising on how frantic and emotional it was in the opening 20 minutes? Certainly it appears to have calmed down a bit since then with Manchester City gaining more control which will delight their head coach Enzo Maresca. There’s a little bit of frustration detectable from the home fans.

Haaland fails to adequately clear a Liverpool corner, looping the ball into the air. Mac Allister tries an ambitious overhead kick, but his attempt is off-target. In the next phase of play, Munoz’s low, long-range strike is gathered by Donnarumma.

City are growing into the game as Cherki clips a searching pass over to Semenyo. The ball is slightly overhit, forcing the winger out too wide, allowing Liverpool to regroup. The hosts fly up the other end, with the busy Munoz running at O’Reilly. The City left-back has to match him stride for stride before conceding a corner.

Gravenberch tries to find Munoz with a threaded pass through City’s backline. However, O’Reilly defends expertly, shielding the ball back to his goalkeeper.

Liverpool need more from Wirtz and Barcola. Both big-money attackers have been on the periphery. With Isak, Gakpo and Szoboszlai all absent, Iraola needs the duo on the pitch to deliver.

Liverpool have been aggressive and on the front foot, but we’re still waiting for a noteworthy chance to be created here at Anfield. City haven’t been spectacular, but they’ve done just about enough so far.

Kerkez fires in a cross and there’s a miscommunication between Guehi and Donnarumma, with the centre-back slicing a clearance instead of allowing the goalkeeper to gather the delivery. Barcola can’t capitalise on the loose ball and City get away with one there.

Let’s not kid ourselves about what we are seeing at the moment. There is a lot of noise but nothing has happened to light a fire and the onus has got to be on Liverpool’s players to step this up considerably. This occasion, more than anything, is crying out for someone to play how the supporters are feeling and it’s not there yet. It’s been tame and Manchester City are, accordingly, comfortable.

City motor forward on the counter through Cherki, whose delightful touch takes him away from Mac Allister. From inside his own half, the Frenchman dribbles to the edge of Liverpool’s penalty area. He attempts to play a one-two with Fernandez, but the pass is cut out by Jacquet.

Manchester City have not got going, as of yet. The defiant message from the club is they would not let the verdict affect them. They have defended well enough but have barely strung a passing sequence together against a Liverpool side who appear be playing off pure emotion.

Gravenberch is bossing this game in midfield. Another powerful run from deep results in a delightful nutmeg on Fernandez, who slips over. Liverpool’s energy has been really impressive. City need to ride out this early storm.

It’s getting heated at Anfield! Mac Allister and Anderson clash sparking a scuffle between both sets of players. It threatened to boil over for a second, but the drama quickly calms down and play resumes after the referee has a word with the two captains.

All fairly difficult to stomach, the Manchester City fans’ performance at kick-off. Inflatable bananas to signify nostalgia for the late 1980s, when these were all the rage after the club’s relegation to Division Two? The City of Sheikh Mansour are about as far removed from the era of Jimmy Frizzell as is possible to imagine, with their colossal wealth enabling cheating on an unprecedented scale. And as for the Poznan during You’ll Never Walk Alone? When Liam Gallagher asks Oasis fans to perform this backwards dance during next year’s tour, I suspect there will not be quite the same take-up.

There’s an early flashpoint as Koumas puts Guehi under serious pressure, causing the defender to fall to the ground and grab the ball with his hands. It’s not a foul and Liverpool are given a free kick. The hosts want Guehi booked and Araujo sprints over to the referee waving an imaginary yellow card, but gets one himself.

Amid all the build-up and backstory to this extraordinary fixture it is remarkable that 21-year-old Lewis Koumas is making his first Premier League start as Liverpool’s makeshift centre-forward. And he has started well.

A spell of Man City possession has slightly quelled the atmosphere. On paper, you would have to say the away side’s starting 11 is superior to Liverpool’s.

Liverpool make a fast start as Gravenberch effortlessly turns Fernandez and Munoz darts inside of O’Reilly. The winger’s shot is smothered by Guehi, but the early signs are encouraging for the hosts.

City get us under way at Anfield. This is one we’ve quite literally all been waiting for.

A roaring rendition of YNWA is bellowed by Anfield, which is in full voice. City players huddle together and go over to clap their fans in a show of solidarity.

In the corner of the stadium, where the Sir Kenny Dalglish Stand meets The Kop, there is a white banner with black paint proclaiming: “A generation of supporters cheated” - none of this is bothering the Manchester City fans, who are going back a generation and have a raft of inflatable bananas. (It was a craze in the 1980s, for you younger readers). Anyway, let’s get on with the game and what an opportunity this is for young Lewis Koumas, who has produced the individual performance of the season so far for Liverpool against Tottenham in the Carabao Cup. He needs to be a scampering, scurrying menace once again.

The Kop has now started a chant of “you cheating b-------” you know what you are. Doubt it will be the last time we hear that this afternoon. They are now singing “going down, going down, going down”.

No chance of hearing the names of the Manchester City players as the team is read out by the PA announcer. He is drowned out by the boos, jeers and whistles from the Liverpool fans. The atmosphere is certainly starting to build.

A re-imagining of Oasis’ Wonderwall at the front of the Kop. “And after all,” the banner reads, “you really robbed us all.”

Andoni Iraola told Sky Sports: “He came back from the international break with an overload. He felt a tight hamstring.

“He tried somehow pushing through training, but he was not feeling 100 per cent.

With just over 15 minutes until kick-off, here’s a recap of the two sides.

Liverpool: Alisson, Araujo, Jacquet, van Dijk, Kerkez, Gravenberch, Mac Allister, Barcola, Wirtz, Munoz, Koumas.

Subs: Mamardashvili, Gomez, Endo, Chiesa, Tsimikas, Frimpong, Nyoni, McConnell, Ngumoha.

Man City: Donnarumma, Matheus Luiz, Dias, Guehi, O’Reilly, Anderson, Fernandez, Semenyo, Cherki, Ndiaye, Haaland.

Subs: Rulli, Kovacic, Doku, Vitor Reis, Gvardiol, Bouaddi, Allan, Khusanov, Lewis.

When asked if the mindset and mood are right for him to do his job, the City boss replied: “Yes. Absolutely. Yes.

“The mood is good, the mindset is good. Now it’s time to start the game - finally!

“It [togetherness] is very important; the mix between the players and the fans, everyone.

“We are away in a complicated environment, a complicated stadium, but we are going to do our best to try to win the game.”

The Manchester City players are out for their warm-up and, dare it be said, they were greeted with apathy by the Liverpool fans. Not even the murmur of a boo when Erling Haaland and Co emerged. It surely will be very different when kick off comes.

The current City players found themselves in a peculiar situation as none of this is their fault, but they’ll be the ones who receive the brunt of abuse from rival fans as the public-facing figures of the club. They’ll need to be braced for a hostile reception at every away ground in England.

However, you can expect Anfield to turn up the heat to one of the highest levels, given how alleged City’s actions have impacted Liverpool’s trophy haul.

Jurgen Klopp’s Liverpool finished second in the 2018-19 season, accumulating a staggering 98 points, while winning 30 matches and losing just once. City incredibly pipped them to the Premier League trophy by one point. A strikingly similar scenario occurred in the 2021-22 campaign, with Liverpool placing as runners-up with 92 points. You guessed it, City had 93.

What’s done is done, and ultimately we are entering a territory of ifs, buts and maybes. However, if City’s appeal against the charges is unsuccessful and the guilty verdict is upheld, then Liverpool would have unfairly missed out on historic success and lifelong memories.

The current City players found themselves in a peculiar situation as none of this is their fault, but they’ll be the ones who receive the brunt of abuse from rival fans as the public-facing figures of the club. They’ll need to be braced for a hostile reception at every away ground in England. However, you can expect Anfield to turn up the heat to one of the highest levels, given the aforementioned landscape and how City’s actions have impacted Liverpool’s trophy haul.

Liverpool bus has arrived to a scene of billowing red smoke and the thousands who have gathered singing “Allez Allez Allez!”

The Liverpool fans have just started singing: “Going down! Going down! Going down!” and it’s incredible to think this could be the last meeting at Anfield between the sides for the foreseeable future.

This was the meeting in English football for the last decade and the quality was never higher than between 2018 and 2022. Over those four seasons, Manchester City amassed 358 points. Liverpool’s total was 357. Incredible how one team ended up with three titles and the other only had one.

The Police operation is in full swing. Drones are flying low up and down Anfield Road and the number of high visibility jackets has increased in the last five minutes. The songs are varying between praise for Liverpool players – Alexis Mac Allister is currently in vogue – and scorn for Manchester City. Definitely more people here now.

Around 30 minutes before the buses are expected to meander down Anfield Road and, already, vantage points are being taken and throats are being cleared. “Should have made it a sham and pineapple,” the company’s official account comments.

THE CHARGES HAVE BEEN DROPPED! ... on pizza for the first 114 Liverpool fans through the door of our Great Homer Street store today tastier than a massive points deduction https://t.co/Yw81xluvrT

The Premier League reveals that City’s owners inflated “sham” sponsorship deals by £830.69m between 2009-10 and 2017-18.

Ferran Soriano, chief executive of City Football Group, appears helpless when questioned about the verdict’s findings at the European Football Clubs’ general assembly in Copenhagen by Sky News.

It later amends the statement to “wherever wrongdoing is established”.

The UAE then warns Andy Burnham that it will pull billions of pounds of investment out of the UK in retaliation for the guilty verdict against City.

City argue that their sponsorship deals were part-funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club’s owners, in their appeal, which claims bank statements and witness accounts provide “irrefutable evidence” to support their case.

The Liverpool head coach was asked for his reaction to City’s guilty verdict in his pre-match press conference and, as with many of his peers, he kept his response brief.

“Uncertainty is not good for anyone involved,” he said. “But there is the process ongoing and we have to be patient like everyone else and see what happens at the end.”

It is the most unlikely Oasis song title for a banner but, in a sea of canvas, the word will jump out from the Kop: Acquiesce.

The simplest flags frequently carry the most profound messages and, on a red background, below Acquiesce is the declaration: “MCFC Cheats”. It has been prepared specially and specifically for the return of domestic football to Anfield.

Given the tone coming out of the Etihad Stadium, nobody will be acquiescing to any alleged wrongdoing, certainly not on Sunday, but minds were made up on Merseyside about how far City had pushed the boundaries in pursuit of success a long time ago.

“There has been a lot of talk about various things,” explains John Gibbons, host of Anfield Wrap, the popular Liverpool podcast. “Manchester City trying to say they are going to be hard done to, but there are no great surprises among Liverpool fans about these charges, are there?

“Everyone who goes to the match, who supports Liverpool, have known all along that a lot of those sponsorship deals looked questionable. Did they pass the smell test? That’s why the atmospheres in the past when City came were always brilliant and I’m expecting it will be the same again.”

So that is why Anfield will be a maelstrom of sound and fury for one of the most significant occasions in Premier League history.

The half-and-half scarves have been replaced by more topical match-day merchandise this afternoon...

Here is what City’s head coach said during his first press conference after the guilty verdict:

“There is a process ongoing and in this moment I completely trust the club … I trust the club because I trust the people and this is also the reason why I joined the club. And then there is not another club in the world where I would [rather] be.”

“Absolutely not. The last time I was here was the treble season. I know the effort from the players, from the club, from the manager in that time that was Pep [Guardiola]. I know exactly the effort that the club put to achieve that kind of target.”

“I won the Championship with Leicester. League One, we will see, but we are thinking about something that we don’t know.”

I’m not worried at all. The environment [among] the players is nice. In this moment we are top of the league so the players have all the reason to be happy and excited.

“One hundred per cent… Because I know the organisation from years ago, and I know how serious they are, I know that they do the right things. I would like to speak about this when we win the appeal.”

While Liverpool have struggled for wins in this fixture of late, it’s worth noting that this run includes five draws.

Liverpool have won just three of their last 13 Premier League clashes with Man City 👀 https://t.co/OxkeDpLjQq

On Saturday Manchester United fans resurrected their “ticker” mocking Manchester City’s trophy drought following their rivals’ cheating scandal:

There was also a nod to Rui Pinto, the whistleblower whose Football Leaks documents prompted the Premier League’s investigation into City:

There were four days between the news leaking that Manchester City had been found guilty of the majority of charges first levelled at them by the Premier League in February 2023 and the independent commission findings dropping.

Staff, then, had had a bit of time to process a guilty verdict although little, it seems, could adequately prepare them for the excoriating tone and content of the commission’s ruling.

“The thing that has shocked me more than anything is the language the commission used to describe the club’s conduct,” one staff member told Telegraph Sport this week.

“We had been waiting for a very long time to see what came out of these Premier League charges and lots of different things go through your head. But I just wasn’t expecting that. I’m still a bit shell-shocked by the ferocity of what the commission said. I think that’s what’s worried me.”

"Enjoy the ride and smile" Erling Haaland with a message for Man City fans ahead of their trip to Anfield this weekend 🎙️🩵 https://t.co/H7so0fk6XE

“The international break is good because we can review what we have done and what we can do better,” Enzo Maresca said after Manchester City’s harum-scarum 5-3 victory over Sunderland. “But at the same time we can relax a little bit more.” One wonders how much respite Enzo Maresca and Manchester City actually enjoyed in the intervening 21 days.

Since City last kicked a football in anger, they have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges levelled at them by the Premier League in a verdict that has shaken professional football to its very core. The club have appealed and the extent of their punishment now rests with an independent panel. Until then, though, the show goes on and City’s players and staff must compete knowing that their every move now comes with a caveat.

City have put up a united front and on Thursday Maresca and Haaland duly delivered the party lines, the City head coach revealing that the feeling among his charges was “fantastic”. “[My players] know what we can control is the football side – they are not worried at all about different things,” Maresca said, before adding that he trusts the club “completely”. The Italian doubled down on his remarks in his Friday press conference.

City maintain their innocence and many of Maresca’s peers have remained tight-lipped on the case, though Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick admitted this week he has questions, while Régis Le Bris urged football’s governing bodies to be “relentless” in safeguarding competitive integrity.

Given all that has happened, it would be easy to forget that this is, for now, a top-of-the-table clash and has been one of the Premier League’s marquee rivalries since the days of Guardiola-Jürgen Klopp. Liverpool fans have never been ones to roll out the red carpet when City are in town, but the ill feeling and belligerence will only intensify at Anfield this time around owing to the events of the past weeks.

City are top of the league having won all five of their league matches so far, while Liverpool have huffed and puffed to sixth, remaining unbeaten.

#1410. Celtic fans disgracefully boo during minute's silence on Remembrance Sunday: Referee ends tribute after just 13 SECONDS - even after warning from the PA announcer

By LUKE AUGUSTUS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 03:28 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 04:51 EST, 9 November 2026

Celtic were forced to curtail plans to commemorate Remembrance Day after a section of their supporters booed during the planned minute's silence on Remembrance Sunday.

The Bhoys hosted Kilmarnock in the Scottish Premiership on Sunday - with Liam Scales' goal proving the difference in a 1-0 win.

However, ahead of kick-off at Parkhead, the annual tribute to the armed forces and their families was overshadowed by some fans' loud jeers.

As the players from both teams gathered around the centre-circle, an announcement on the public address system said: 'We will have a minute's silence today on Remembrance Sunday to remember all victims of all conflicts. We remember, in particular, the men who served Celtic football club and lost their lives at wartime.'

The audible disdain resulted in referee John Beaton being forced to cut the silence after just 13 seconds.

The noise was so palpable that the Celtic TV broadcast turned down the volume to try and minimise its impact too.

The minute's silence ahead of Celtic versus Kilmarnock was cut short due to some fans booing

Celtic TV turned down the volume to try and minimise the jeers during the curtailed silence

Referee John Beaton (right) cut the minute's silence after 13 seconds as a result of the booing

Furthermore, the lower tier of the standing section was empty until the Green Brigade and other fans started to file in from the concourse when referee Beaton’s whistle signalled the end of the tribute.

Football clubs across the United Kingdom observe a minute's silence with their nearest home fixture around Remembrance Sunday and Armistice Day - with the latter on November 11.

Many teams also wear poppies, something Kilmarnock wore on their strip, but Celtic didn't.

Some Celtic supporters refuse to partake in the tradition or actively take a stance against it, often citing the club’s Irish roots and linking it to the British Army‘s role in The Troubles.

Last season, in a quirk, Celtic hosted Kilmarnock on Remembrance Sunday too - with that minute's silence also cut short due to jeering. That time referee Don Robertson cut it short at 15 seconds.

As well as the booing in that match last term, some fans turned their back on the minute's silence and also made gestures.

Sunday's 1-0 win over Kilmarnock sees Celtic regain their four-point lead at the top of the Scottish Premiership.

It was under-pressure Martin O'Neill's side's first league win in their last three games.

Scales scored the only goal of the game on 26 minutes when he hooked a Camilo Duran cross into the top corner.

Celtic fans show their displeasure during the minute's silence for Remembrance Day in 2025

Celtic - and Kasper Hogh in particular - otherwise had a frustrating day in front of goal, with Benjamin Nygren missing a second-half penalty.

Hogh had an early goal disallowed as his barren run without a goal hit the 16-game mark since he netted a hat-trick at Kilmarnock on his second appearance.

Celtic have 31 points from their opening 13 matches - four more than bitter rivals Rangers who sit second but have a game in hand.

Kilmarnock remain rooted to the bottom of the table with nine points from 13 games - two adrift of 11th-place Aberdeen who have played a match fewer.

#1409. See a tardigrade shed its skin — October’s best science images

The month’s sharpest science shots, selected by Nature’s photo team.

Gonzalo Quiroga Artigas/Nikon Small World

Gonzalo Quiroga Artigas/Nikon Small World

Just another day in space. NASA’s Astrobee, a cubic robot around 30 centimetres across, is designed to work in the microgravity environment inside the International Space Station (ISS). Each of NASA’s three Astrobees — working autonomously, or controlled by ISS astronauts or Earth-bound flight controllers and researchers —  float around taking on tasks such as drawing up inventories and recording experiments. The robots also function as experimental subjects to test microgravity software and hardware.

The Canadian-built arm of the ISS, Canadarm2, holds a Cygnus XL cargo spacecraft during undocking operations. It was released about 420 kilometres above the North Atlantic Ocean on 9 October.

Sting mechanics. A bee’s stinger was observed in action as it injected its venom, called apitoxin, into a gel that mimics skin1. Fiorella Ramirez-Esquivel, a sensory ecologist at the University of New South Wales in Canberra, and her collaborators detached the stinger from a honey bee (Apis mellifera) and studied the mechanics of its pumping mechanism. They discovered that it involves two collapsible cylinders that act as pistons.

Mourning ritual. In northwestern Namibia, Italian photographer Federico Veronesi followed tracks on a dry river bed to catch a rare glimpse of an elephant carrying a dead calf. His shot was the overall winner of the 2026 Wildlife Photographer of the Year competition, which is developed and produced by the Natural History Museum, London. Researchers have documented a range of mourning behaviours in African elephants (Loxodonta spp.), including carrying and guarding the dead.

Federico Veronesi/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Oscar Whitfield/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Oscar Whitfield/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Tony Wu/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Tony Wu/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Agorastos Papatsanis/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Agorastos Papatsanis/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Francisco Negroni/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Francisco Negroni/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

A dung beetle (unidentified species) in Zimbabwe’s Zambezi National Park shot by Oscar Whitfield, who won the Young Wildlife Photographer of the Year competition.

Photo naturalist Tony Wu spent three years tracking the behaviour of eels off Japan’s southern island of Kyushu. Eventually he captured two specimens of Abbott’s moray eel (Gymnothorax eurostus) in what could be the first photo documenting their spawning behaviour. He used a red light, because the animals spawn at night and are sensitive to other colours of light. On his blog, he wrote that this was “the most difficult and challenging photographic endeavor that I have ever undertaken”.

Nature photographer Agorastos Papatsanis shone ultraviolet light on the forest floor at the foot of Mount Olympus in Greece to reveal the glowing stems of beautiful bonnet mushrooms (Mycena renati). Many fungi fluoresce under UV light — an effect that mycologists can use to help identify species.

Chilean photographer Francisco Negroni took this image of a dead puma (Puma concolor) displayed as a hunting trophy on a fence in the Patagonia region of Argentina.

The Wildlife Photographer of the Year exhibition is on until 11 July 2027 at London’s Natural History Museum.

Beautiful tech. This unusual view, of droplets of ink being squeezed through nozzles and onto paper during the printing process, won first place in the 2026 Nikon Small World competition. Ole Bielfeldt, an experimental photographer in Cologne, Germany, was partially motivated by his desire to understand how inkjet printers work.

Satu Paavonsalo & Dr. Sinem Karaman/Nikon Small World

Satu Paavonsalo & Dr. Sinem Karaman/Nikon Small World

Dr. Gonzalo Quiroga Artigas/Nikon Small World

Dr. Gonzalo Quiroga Artigas/Nikon Small World

Pierre Nouaux & Laurent Kodjabachian, Camille Boutin/Nikon Small World

Pierre Nouaux & Laurent Kodjabachian, Camille Boutin/Nikon Small World

Brandon Antonio Segura Torres & Priscilla Vieto Bonilla, Paula Alejandra Olivera/Nikon Small World

Brandon Antonio Segura Torres & Priscilla Vieto Bonilla, Paula Alejandra Olivera/Nikon Small World

This mesmerizing web is a cross-section of a mouse eye, showing retinal blood vessels and the optic nerve.

A tardigrade moulting and laying an egg in the old skin.

Skin cells from embryonic Xenopus frogs, show cilia (green), centrioles (a type of organelle, red) and cell membranes (white).

The nuclei in this 20-day-old sea urchin larva fluoresce blue to create a doodle-like outline.

A seal louse (Antarctophthirus sp.) attached to a hair from one of the aquatic mammals.

First responders. Rescuers carry an adult female orangutan (Pongo pygmaeus) across a palm-oil plantation in Laman Satong, Indonesian Borneo, on 30 September. Indonesia has been experiencing its worst wildfire season in a decade, blanketing southeast Asia in thick smoke.

Maria D. Guillén/IPHES-CERCA/Antonio Rodríguez-Hidalgo

Maria D. Guillén/IPHES-CERCA/Antonio Rodríguez-Hidalgo

Maria D. Guillén/IPHES-CERCA/Antonio Rodríguez-Hidalgo

Maria D. Guillén/IPHES-CERCA/Antonio Rodríguez-Hidalgo

Neanderthal hand. A dig in a cave in northern Spain has yielded the remains of a 46,000-year-old Neanderthal, including a well-preserved hand. The findings, which were presented in Tarragona, Spain, on 19 October and have not yet been peer reviewed, included analyses of what researchers described as well-preserved ancient DNA.

Space jellyfish. The 13 October launch of a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida produced this mesmerizing show as the exhaust glistened in predawn sunlight, and was caught by NASA photographer Bill White. The rocket was headed to the ISS on a resupply mission.

Storm vision. As Typhoon Surigae lingered off the coast of Japan on 28 September, the European Space Agency’s Copernicus Sentinel-1 pictured the sea underneath it using polarized radar. The orange in this false-colour image reveals rough surface conditions caused by strong winds; the calmer seas at the eye of the storm are dark blue.

Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2026), processed by ESA

Underwater treasure trove. A stunning 57 new marine species and 5 genera spanning corals, sea cucumbers and crustaceans were identified in just two weeks at an international ‘species discovery’ workshop in Buenos Aires in July. Scientists from across Latin America and Europe gathered to study marine samples, many of which were collected by the deep-sea remotely operated vehicle SuBastian in an expedition led by the Schmidt Ocean Institute to Argentina’s Mar del Plata Canyon in August 2025. The new species include ‘Loki’, a pale sea cucumber with a blob-like body that features two stubby appendages (Peniagone sp.).

#1408. Xabi Alonso was brought in to end the chaos at Chelsea and he is failing. PLUS: Football's most vanilla pundit gives out-of-his-depth Michael Carrick an easy ride: IAN LADYMAN on My Football Weekend

Published: 07:00 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 07:55 EST, 9 November 2026

The whiff of Premier League failure is in the air as the smoke clears from Bonfire Night.

It always feels this way by the time we get to the November international break.

Managers and their players have had time to settle in and teething problems no longer cut it as a reason for autumn struggles.

Worst of all, Christmas is coming and we all know what tends to happen to teams who are struggling as the end of the year nears.

So at places like Manchester United, Crystal Palace, Sunderland, Newcastle and Spurs there is anxiety about expectations not being met.

Xabi Alonso was hired to break the cycle at Chelsea and he is not yet succeeding

Xabi Alonso's side would appear to be the team that is failing without anybody seeming to notice.

At Stamford Bridge, the environment is conducive to Alonso and his team doing well this season.

Chelsea – not in Europe after last season's troubles – are only playing once a week. So Alonso – hired for his coaching reputation – has time on the grass with players who should arrive every weekend with freshness in their legs.

It's the environment that enabled Michael Carrick to fool everyone at Manchester United last season. While the rest of the Premier League got bogged down in the schedule, United sailed upwards on the back of a lighter load.

When we look at Alonso's team we see only familiar Chelsea things – and not in a good way.

Inconsistent tactics, some strange selections and, on the back of it, some very ordinary results.

This is the cycle Alonso was hired to break and he is not yet succeeding.

Sunday's defeat to Sunderland can be added to league setbacks against Spurs, Brentford and Arsenal.

They were unimpressive in beating United a couple of weeks ago also. Carrick's team outplayed them in the first half and should have been two or three goals ahead.

Under Alonso, Chelsea are yet to establish an identity or discernible patterns. It is hard to know yet what his best back four (or five) looks like. In the absence of the injured striker Joao Pedro, Alonso seems happier to play without one rather than use Danny Welbeck, signed for just this scenario in the summer.

The absence of Joao Pedro is significant while Alonso is also without his first choice goalkeeper Emi Martinez. These things matter.

But Chelsea have a huge squad of international players. Maybe it's too big. Whatever the case Alonso must get the best out of it soon.

Nobody seems to be talking about how very underwhelming the whole thing feels. But if it continues, they soon will be.

On Match of the Day on Sunday night, football's most vanilla pundit Dion Dublin was asked whether Michael Carrick has done enough to keep his job.

'I think so,' said Dublin. 'I think Michael has all the tools but the players just aren't doing what they need to do.'

At every other club in the Premier League, under-performing players and the bad results that tend to follow lead to intense scrutiny and criticism of the manager. It's his job to affect these things.

Not at United, though, where the level of public and media support for Carrick remains extraordinary and illogical.

If we applied this level of leeway to everybody else then nobody would ever be sacked.

Dion Dublin, pictured on Homes Under The Hammer duty, gave Michael Carrick an easy ride

Carrick is out of his depth at sinking Manchester United - his team are a shambles

Yes, there are a number of factors at play at Old Trafford. Yes, we know what they are and who is to blame for them. Yes, it's a very difficult job.

But the truth is that Carrick is failing in a quite spectacular fashion.

Of all the managers to have followed Sir Alex Ferguson over the last 13 and a half years, Erik ten Hag was the one who looked most out of his depth in terms of the chaotic nature of his team's football.

Carrick is now on the way to eclipsing that. His team are a shambles and that's on him. Once again, this is a mediocre league and it's quite criminal that Carrick has his group of players in the bottom three.

The former Middlesbrough manager is so out of his depth it's quite painful to watch.

It was another extraordinary afternoon at Old Trafford as United drew 4-4 with Aston Villa.

Unai Emery's Villa team is going through yet another regeneration after the sale of big-name players in the summer and balancing the Champions League with domestic football will once again be a challenge.

Emery seems to have made his mind up about one of his squad members, though, after former United and Chelsea winger Alejandro Garnacho was left out of the squad entirely yesterday.

Garnacho is a talented player but has made only 14 Premier League starts – and none at Villa – since leaving Old Trafford for Chelsea in the summer of 2025.

The Argentine is still only 22 so time is on his side but at some point he is going to have to do something on the field to justify the investment in a career that is currently going nowhere.

Alejandro Garnacho was left out of the squad entirely yesterday by Aston Villa

Sky's excellent touchline reporter Patrick Davison had his work cut out post-match at Old Trafford as he interviewed one manager in danger of the sack and another who had just flounced down the tunnel like a chap with his pants on fire.

Neither Michael Carrick nor Unai Emery seemed particularly comfortable in the face of Davison's questions and that's exactly as it should be.

He is there to ask questions on behalf of a broadcaster that ploughs billions of pounds into our national sport each year. He is not there to apply soothing balm.

There would appear to be many others happy to do that anyway.

Sky's Patrick Davison (right) is not there to apply soothing balm with his questions

Less impressive was the appearance of Sky's latest metric that appeared on screen during Nottingham Forest's dismantling of Manchester City on Saturday.

Titled simply 'pressures' it indicated that Forest were doing rather better at it than City.

But what did it mean? Does anybody know? Or indeed care?

Two seasons ago at the City Ground I saw local boy Ryan Yates give Casemiro such a chasing as Forest beat Manchester United that the great Brazilian was taken off before he was sent off.

On Saturday by the river, Yates made his first league start of the season as Oliver Glasner’s team overwhelmed City.

Beforehand Yates gave an address to his team-mates. He told them about what it meant to play for the club and touched briefly on its history.

He told me once in an interview that he tends to tell all new arrivals at Forest what the two stars on the shirt actually mean – two European Cups won in 1979 and 1980.

It’s smart work by a lad who knows what football means in Nottingham and it was smart work by his manager who knew that his team needed an injection of something visceral to drag him from a trough of failure that was threatening to cost him his job.

Manchester United could probably do with a bit of that right now. So, possibly, could Chelsea and indeed Tottenham. At Liverpool, they lament the absence from the team of Trent Alexander-Arnold and Curtis Jones.

It takes an awful lot to make up a Premier League team these days. Place of birth is not a priority any more and that’s understandable. But sometimes it helps.

When was the last time an English team won the title with a poor goalkeeper?

Flick back over the last couple of decades and it's hard to find an example.

So what hope for Manchester City this season?

Gianluigi Donnarumma is anything but a poor goalkeeper but the problem is that he is playing like one and it is there that City's current problems start.

Enzo Maresca's back four looks shot to pieces and that often happens when they lose faith in the chap behind them.

Maresca says he won't change. 'My team is Gigi plus ten others,' is his take.

Enzo Maresca says he will not change goalkeeper despite Gianluigi Donnarumma's problems

His back up is 34-year-old Argentinean Geronimo Rulli, a member of his country's World Cup squad with nine caps to his name.

Rulli is well-travelled and has some pedigree. He was, for example, Villarreal's hero as they beat Manchester United in a Europa League final shoot out in 2021.

If Maresca trusts him then maybe now is the time to show it. If he doesn't then why did City sign him?

Liverpool goalkeeper Alisson is perhaps not quite what he once was at the age of 34 but produced a throwback performance for his team at Crystal Palace. Without him, Liverpool would not have won.

Nevertheless Palace's struggles go on and their coach Pierre Sage is in danger of losing his job.

However the south London club cannot say they were not warned about trouble ahead.

Former manager Oliver Glasner spent most of last season in a huff about what he saw as a failure by the Palace board to invest properly in the squad.

Palace have won twice in ten Premier League games this season and it seems Glasner may have been right.

Brighton continue to fly high and to produce such an energetic performance to beat Brentford having played away at Getafe in Europe on Thursday was testimony to the fitness of Fabian Hurzeler's squad.

The Seagulls were certainly helped by having to play against ten for an hour, though, and on Match of the Day the enduringly listenable Jonathan Pearce spoke for all of us as he watched Chema Andres go down after minimal contact to his cheek from Brentford's Igor Thiago.

'That was nothing, nothing, nothing,' said Pearce as Thiago walked off.

Coming so soon after theatrics from Alexis MacAllister and Gabriel in the Liverpool-Arsenal game last week, the issue of players exaggerating facial contact to get opponents sent off remains a live one.

Brentford's manager Keith Andrews was measured on the issue but suggested the tactic was becoming 'a game within a game'.

It's a problem and referees head Howard Webb needs his officials to get a grip of it.

Brighton's Pascal Gross has now created more than 25 chances for team-mates this season and that's more than anyone else in the Premier League.

Gross cost £1.2million when he returned to the club from Borussia Dortmund last January.

Pascal Gross scored on Sunday and has now created more than 25 chances for team-mates

Bournemouth, meanwhile, cast their net as widely as anybody these days and that includes all the way down the English pyramid.

The South Coast club – on an eight-match winning streak now under Marco Rose – have a relationship with yesterday's FA Cup giant killers Wimborne from the seventh tier.

Wimborne of the Southern League Premier South beat League Two Crawley in Round One and will this week send their Chilean teenage striker Angel Diaz for a trial at the Premier League club.

Story of last season in the EFL was probably Lincoln City's promotion to the Championship where, after 15 games, they are just about keeping their heads above water in 21st place.

Architect of that incredible rise was former futsal coach Michael Skubala who rather sullied the romantic feel of it all by quitting almost immediately to join Bristol City.

This weekend Skubala's team were thrashed 5-0 at home by Norwich with the home fans singing that their manager would be 'sacked in the morning'.

Lincoln have already won at Ashton Gate, back in September, at the start of a run that has seen City win just two from ten.

Sometimes, it really does pay just to stay where you are.

#1407. Painful Coventry defeat will send shudder of fear through Newcastle

Newcastle United suffered a painful, chastening defeat, comprehensively beaten by Coventry City in a performance that should send a shudder of fear through Tyneside.

It was a dreadful night for the visitors, who conceded four goals for the second successive away game. The manner in which they fell apart was damning. Whatever the supposed style of play, it is not good to watch: long balls are pumped forward for short strikers to chase or compete for in the air against far taller centre-backs. Away from home, it is becoming ineffective.

Newcastle are too easy to create chances against and there is not much that gets you excited when they attack.

Matthias Jaissle’s side did create chances against Coventry, but are not clinical and do not inspire confidence they can be with the players they have. Defensively, they escaped earlier in the season, but are now being exposed and punished. “Not good enough in both boxes,” was Jaissle’s blunt verdict. “To concede eight goals in two away games is not good enough.”

Matthias Jaissle on this evening's defeat at the Coventry Building Society Arena. https://t.co/216NW6Laz8

Newcastle’s misery was in stark contrast to the joyous celebrations from Coventry. This was a thoroughly deserved first home win of the season for Frank Lampard’s side.

“It was an outstanding performance,” the manager said. “We knew we would have to suffer at times against a team like Newcastle. But we were really good at the basics, winning the second balls, winning the duels, those moments are critical. It’s not always about pretty patterns, it’s about work ethic.”

The win lifts Coventry level on points with Manchester United and will give them fresh confidence at this level. This could be the start of something special for them.

As for Newcastle, this raises uncomfortable questions about their summer recruitment, with so many expensive players on the bench or playing badly. It also means people will query whether Jaissle’s implementation of “vertical football” is working. The fact Lampard talked so openly about winning the duels to set up the win will anger the German.

A win for Newcastle United this evening will take Matthias Jaissle’s side up to fourth in the Premier League and vindicate the members of the club’s hierarchy who insisted they had appointed an elite manager to replace Eddie Howe.

It will also suggest they got their summer rebuild right and everything will point to an exciting future for a new look team.

Yet, should Newcastle lose against a Coventry City side – newly promoted to the top flight and yet to win at home this season – ripples of discontent will spread through the fanbase and everything about the summer, from managerial appointment to player recruitment will be called into question.

That may seem like an odd thing to write given how wildly different those reactions are but that is where Newcastle find themselves at the moment. We do not actually know if they are any good or what the expectations should be for a young team with a rookie Premier League head coach.

There remains an undercurrent of anxiety among supporters who have seen so many of their best players leave over the last 12 months and be replaced by young, emerging talent from across Europe.

The 4-1 thrashing at Leeds in their last away game was a painful reminder of the team’s vulnerability. They were bullied and outclassed.

Newcastle have not put together an impressive 90-minute performance since the opening day draw with Liverpool, yet that defeat to Leeds was also the only game they have lost. in all competitions. We will know a lot more about them after this. This is a game they are expected to win, so the ramifications of a defeat will be more severe.

When Brian Kilcline was at Notts County, the manager Jimmy Sirrel became a little perturbed by the nickname his young centre-back had carried since his school days. It might have been nice alliteration, but “Killer Kilcline” was not exactly the image he wanted his team to portray.

“Also the lads shouting, ‘get him Killer’ tended to alert referees,” Kilcline recalls.

So Sirrel decided he would put it to the County fans. He organised a competition to establish a better moniker for his foursquare defender.

“You know what they came up with?” Kilcline says. “Curly Wurly. Like the chocolate bar. It was to do with my hair, which was naturally curled. By the way, it was never a perm. But I mean, come on. I can’t imagine Curly Wurly would have intimidated anyone.”

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Coventry City and Newcastle United from the Ricoh Arena. Newcastle have played only once there in the league – a 4-1 victory in the Championship back in 2010 when Chris Hughton’s side stormed the league. Their last top-flight visit to the city was way back in 2000, the year Cov’s 34-season spell in the top division ended. Alan Shearer Kevin Gallacher scored at Highfield Road on that occasion, a year after they were sent packing 4-1 by Gordon Strachan’s side by virtue of goals from Carlton Palmer, Paul Williams, Robbie Keane and Mustapha Hadji.

Today’s visit begins with Newcastle in 11th, having bounced back from their Monday night mauling at Elland Road to beat Hull 23 days ago. So bunched is the table, though, that victory tonight would propel them up to fourth. Coventry, by contrast, are 19th after one win and four defeats from their opening five games. If they win they would join Manchester United on six points and leap to 14th, one place ahead of Nottingham Forest, the team they beat last time out before the international break.

Frank Lampard’s side responded superbly after being hammered 5-0 by Brighton in their last home game, tightening up in midfield and defence and finding precisely Forest’s weak spots that Oliver Glasner has been unable so far to armour-plate. Taiwo Awoniyi, who was sent off during that defeat by Brighton, is absent serving the second leg of his three-match suspension and Hajii Wright and Aurele Amenda are still some way off returning. Tino Livramento pulled out of the England camp with injury and is likely to be sidelined for a while longer but Matthias Jaissle was more optimistic about his raft of other doubts: William Osula, Lewis Miley, Amar Dedic, club captain Dan Burn, Anthony Elanga and Jacob Ramsey.

#1406. Declan Rice reveals he's stepped back from social media because it can 'ruin your whole day' after sick trolling of him and his girlfriend - as he poses in new photoshoot

By LUKE AUGUSTUS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 06:36 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 08:45 EST, 9 November 2026

Declan Rice has opened up about reducing his use of social media - citing the mental toll it can have.

The Arsenal and England midfielder has been subjected to online abuse in the past - with his long-term partner Lauren Fryer having also been targeted.

Online abuse about her appearance had led to Fryer wiping all posts from her Instagram page back in 2024.

While Rice still has an Instagram account, he quit X three years ago as a result of the negativity that app can bring.

'I've not been back on the app since,' he told GQ Magazine - after being named among their Men of the Year. 'You could be having a great morning. You read one thing, and it just ruins your whole day.

'I feel like that's one of my strongest points... the ability to block out noise and not deal with that kind of stuff.'

Declan Rice has revealed he quit X three years ago due to the abuse he would receive online

Rice and long-term partner Lauren Fryer have been targeted in the past (pair pictured with their son Jude in May)

The midfielder says one post could 'ruin' his whole day - even if he was a great day beforehand

Rice, who has a four-year-old son called Jude with Fryer, is worried about the impact of social media on the younger generations.

'Screen time, for me, isn't a big thing,' he says of his own personal phone usage. 'I think social media for kids is 100 per cent a problem. I don't feel like there's as much personality now as there was a few years ago.'

As detailed by Daily Mail Sport last month, the 27-year-old is closing in on a new long-term deal at Arsenal believed to be worth around £350,000 per week.

The contract will put him on a level footing with Bukayo Saka at the top of the club's salary list.

And speaking about money in football as a whole, Rice told GQ Magazine that the finances within the sport are 'ridiculous' and despite his wealth he still wants to set a good example to his son Jude.

'The money that's in football as a whole is just ridiculous,' he continued. 'It's important to understand what things cost, even if you don't have to worry about paying for them.

'You still want to teach your kid values, not wanting them to be spoiled. You want them to work and to understand the value of life and money.

'It makes you more comfortable to be able to do things. But I don't wake up and think, "Oh, I've got loads of money", it's not the end goal.'

The 27-year-old is worried about the pitfalls of social media on the younger generations

The 27-year-old Arsenal and England star has been named in GQ Magazine's Men of the Year

Rice's focus will now be on his country with England hosting Croatia on Thursday night in the UEFA Nations League before travelling to World Cup champions Spain on Sunday.

Going into the November international break, the midfielder is enjoying a fine season with Arsenal who sit six points clear at the top of the Premier League with 27 points from their opening 10 matches.

#1405. Ecosystems depend on people: don’t abandon them

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

The abandonment of villages in Japan is changing ecosystems. Studies are finding that biodiversity has declined in places that people have left behind.Credit: Tomohiro Ohsumi/Bloomberg/Getty

The idea that humanity is separate from the rest of the planet is deep-rooted, but wrong. Indeed, for most of human history, this has not been the case1. Many landscapes seen by European colonists as ‘wilderness’ were in fact tended by Indigenous people. This includes North America’s wildflower-studded oak savannahs and Australia’s fire-maintained ecosystems. Worldwide, traditional agricultural practices — which have been used for millennia, in some cases2 — have created ecological niches that support insects, amphibians, birds and plants, many of which have evolved together with humans.

When humans disappear, biodiversity takes a surprising turn

When humans disappear, biodiversity takes a surprising turn

People have always cleared land to some extent. But the scale of this practice has been unprecedented since the beginning of industrialization in the mid-eighteenth century, and especially since the onset of industrial farming. Intensive land conversion is the biggest driver of biodiversity loss. It’s a key reason why countries agreed four years ago to protect 30% of land and water habitats by 2030 (also called the 30 × 30 target).

That goal, however, explicitly did not intend for protected areas to be human-free zones3. Now, as Nature reports in a News feature, evidence is emerging that biodiversity does not necessarily thrive in places that humans leave behind. In Japan, where entire villages are being abandoned because of rural depopulation, the decline in traditional rice-farming practices and woodland management is reducing habitat availability for many birds, insects and plants that thrive in flooded paddies, along field margins or in open-canopy forests.

This example and others show that protected areas need humans to be responsible for specific tasks. These jobs include water management, the provision of grazing animals and ecologically informed forestry, such as using prescribed burning to prevent catastrophic megafires similar to those the world is seeing increasingly. The Americas, Europe and Australia will need many thousands of fire-trained professionals in the coming decades.

Protecting nature means valuing biodiversity

Protecting nature means valuing biodiversity

Land-tending practices also include traditional foraging and planting, the building of clam gardens on the coast and cutting down trees and shrubs to thin woodlands and stimulate fresh growth. Such work must be informed by modern ecology and conservation biology — which increasingly incorporate lessons from ecological knowledge that comes from, in some cases, millennia of practical field experiments.

These practices also need to be funded. Traditional farming and land-management techniques are expensive compared with industrial agriculture, which requires less labour and has huge yields. If humanity wants to preserve these traditional relationships with the planet and the biodiversity they support, governments will have to subsidize this work directly.

This is already being done in a limited way, through grants to farmers and in agricultural-biodiversity schemes. However, nations should consider providing robust and comprehensive support. Programmes could be based on the US Civilian Conservation Corps — created during the Great Depression in the 1930s — although standards would need to be updated to improve diversity and equity, and activities would have to be supported by evidence.

Biodiversity conservation has an evidence problem — it’s time to fix it

Biodiversity conservation has an evidence problem — it’s time to fix it

At a time of mass unemployment in the private sector, the corps was a publicly funded job-creation scheme that employed three million young men. Working in teams, they planted trees, prepared terraced fields, built roads and trails, erected fire towers and otherwise tended to US natural resources between 1933 and 1942.

Today, artificial intelligence is raising concerns not only about its environmental impacts4, but also that it could cause another phase of high levels of unemployment. Governments looking to establish schemes that could buffer their workforces against job losses associated with technological changes should consider investing in people’s relationships with land, water and biodiversity. It would be a mutually beneficial outcome: for people and the ecosystems we inhabit.

#1404. Wayne Rooney and Paddy McGuinness laud football super-agent Paul Stretford - who has worked with Man United icon since his teens - at star-studded Global Football Industry Awards

Published: 13:14 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 13:15 EST, 9 November 2026

Wayne Rooney has led the praise for football super-agent Paul Stretford as the industry heavyweight was honoured at the Global Football Industry Awards.

Stretford, alongside Kenneth Shepherd, received the prestigious Lifetime Achievement Award at this year's Awards in recognition of their longstanding careers and work on Soccer Aid for Unicef.

He has worked by Rooney's side for more than 20 years, and has recently appeared on the former footballer's reality TV show, which he fronts alongside wife Coleen.

Rooney presented Stretford with the award himself, alongside Toni Duggan and comedian Paddy McGuinness. Theo Walcott and Jamie Carragher hosted the ceremony.

Rooney said of his agent and close friend: 'Paul in particular has had a major influence on my life since I was a teenager and has guided my career.

'Both Paul and Kenneth are very deserving of this award. It is not before time and I'm delighted for both of them. The work they've done on Soccer Aid is phenomenal too.'

Wayne Rooney (centre) has lauded close friend and football super agent Paul Stretford (right)

Stretford doesn't just look after Rooney, having also worked with the likes of Harry Maguire since founding Proactive Sports Management, now known as Triple S Sports Group, in 1987.

Shepherd, meanwhile, has been instrumental in the success of the Soccer Aid initiative which has raised more than £137million for Unicef since it launched in 2006.

McGuinness added: 'I'm so proud to pay tribute to a duo who have had a profound impact on football and two figures we've both had the pleasure of working with over the years. Together, they built the Triple S Group into a dynamic force in British and international football.'

England assistant manager Anthony Barry also carried out an exclusive Q&A at the event, which saw Tyler Alexander-Arnold, brother of England defender Trent, also scoop a top award.

The brother of the Real Madrid star represents Jordan Henderson, Jarrod Bowen and Andy Robertson as well as his sibling, who saw his PLG Agency bought by Gersh talent agency in May of this year.
