Under normal circumstances there would be a high level of anticipation around this game, even though it is the eighth time in 11 seasons that City and PSG have faced each other in the Champions League. But given the backdrop of City guilty verdict and it being the first home fixture since that announcement it is even more fascinating. There will also be, of course, Pep Guardiola back “in his house”, as his successor, Enzo Maresca. put it. The atmosphere will be interesting.

If the verdicts are upheld, of course, it wasn’t their penthouse and it wasn’t their caviar.

We got to live in a penthouse and eat caviar for 15 years and if we have to go back to a semi in the suburbs, well, fine.

When Manchester City endured their first major sanction over financial fair play in 2014, the biggest club accused alongside them that summer were Paris St-Germain, another Champions League arriviste who had been raised from mediocrity to the elite by some frantic spending from a Middle East fossil fuel dynasty.

Then, 12 years ago, both sides bitterly opposed the Uefa sanctions imposed on them – although they eventually agreed to the terms. Now, they face one another in Manchester with PSG aiming for a third consecutive Champions League title, and City fighting for their lives in the face of an overwhelming guilty verdict for nine years of Premier League rule-breaking.

Both clubs are transformed from the entities that their current owners acquired. While PSG now find themselves at the centre of the new order in European football, City are once again on the outside.

Whatever the outcome of this process, I won’t forget the connection and relationships I had here. It will never be erased.

Good evening, and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League tie between Manchester City and Paris St-Germain, champions in 2025 and 2026 and favourites to become only the fourth club, after Real Madrid (who have done it twice), Ajax and Bayern Munich to win a hat-trick of European Cups.

After Manchester City’s conviction by an independent commission on 114 charges of financial malpractice in contravention of Premier League rules, finding the right tone to use to cover their matches during their appeal is difficult. While they are in limbo, the rest of English football is in purgatory and although Gary Neville, the Pope of Pilsworth, in unsurprisingly hyperbolic fashion has said he would prefer not to cover City’s games in future, that is not an indulgence a serious news organisation would countenance. They have to be covered and the issues addressed.

Having said that, in this format of a rolling report on the old minute-by-minute template, I think we have to cover the controversy and its implications in the whole during the build-up and keep an eye on reaction and references to it during the run of play. But I don’t think it would serve anyone to take the stance during the live coverage that anything that is happening on the field is unimportant, redundant and ultimately void because of the guilty verdicts, and hence adopt a flippant tone. I propose once the match starts to treat it as a match while not ignoring the context.

Right, let’s get stuck into the Gulf State sovereign wealth fund derby… sorry, imposible to resist.

#1390. AI agents enter the ‘wet lab’

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

James Zou is in the Department of Biomedical Data Science, Stanford University, Stanford, California 94305, USA.

Artificial intelligence has been tremendously useful in science, but, most of the time, it is used for computational work, such as analysing data, making predictions and scouring literature. Carrying out ‘wet laboratory’ experiments — which involve handling liquids, biological material and chemicals — is another matter. An AI system might design a promising biologically active molecule in minutes, but testing it can take weeks or months and requires extensive human effort. In a paper published in Nature, Wu et al.1 introduce AutoDNA, a lab in which AI agents plan and conduct molecular-biology experiments involving DNA, with relatively little human intervention. The work shows how AI systems can begin to close the gap between proposing an experiment and doing it.

#1389. Pierre Sage’s Lyon return ends in disappointment for Crystal Palace

Pierre Sage felt Crystal Palace were “really far off” his expectations after suffering a 3-2 away Europa League defeat by his former side Lyon.

Corentin Tolisso opened the scoring for the hosts and Ernest Nuamah doubled Lyon’s advantage late in a first half devoid of any shots on target for the visitors.

Yéremy Pino halved the deficit five minutes after the break, before Pavel Sulc restored the two-goal lead, and substitute Daichi Kamada’s late goal proved a mere consolation.

“At the end, we were frustrated by the result, but in the first half we have to be frustrated in the way we play,” said Sage, speaking to PalaceTV.

“I think we didn’t play this first half. We are really far off our standards in the mental side of the play, in the tactical side of the play, because the players are too high between our lines and we really struggled a lot with that.

“When you give back the ball to your opponent, you suffer a lot and we were better in the second half. You cannot win this kind of game by playing only one half.”

Sage’s side got the better of his predecessor, Oliver Glasner, after they bounced back to beat Nottingham Forest 3-1 at Selhurst Park on Sunday.

After that victory, the Frenchman called for more consistency from his team, but on Thursday night was left ruing missed opportunities and goals conceded too easily by last season’s Conference League winners.

Sage was sacked by Lyon in January 2025 after a 14-month spell with the Ligue 1 outfit. Like Glasner’s, his own reunion ended in disappointment.

He told Uefa: “It’s a very disappointing return because we lost. I can’t take satisfaction from coming back home or seeing familiar faces when the result isn’t there.

“The scoreline may have been close, but there was a big difference in the way the two teams played.

“We improved considerably after the break and gave ourselves a chance, but conceding that third goal made things difficult.

“I think our second-half efforts deserved an equaliser, although winning would have been a generous reward given that we only really played [to our level] for one half.”

The veteran captain said: “It has been a long time coming. The fans were up for it, the players were up for it so we’re very happy with the performance.”

When asked about Evanilson’s header, which Smith supplied the assist for, he replied: “It wasn’t my best cross but I put it in an area, what a finish from him and I think we deserved that little bit of luck.

“From there on we went on to win the game but in the second half we got a little bit tired but the quality that came off the bench is great and we look forward to Sunday now.

“It’s a great header, he deserved it because he has worked very hard this season and many more to come from him.”

Palace manager Pierre Sage managed Lyon between November 2023 and January 2025, and another sub-plot is American businessman John Textor’s involvement with the French club. #1388. Rise of Germanic and Celtic languages is written in ancient DNA

In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Aghascrebagh Ogham Stone in Northern Ireland shows much-worn inscriptions.Credit: Radharc Images/Alamy

More than one billion people worldwide speak Germanic languages such as English, German and Dutch, whereas Celtic languages — including Welsh, Irish and Gaelic — are spoken by only two or three million people, mostly in northern Europe.

A pair of studies analysing more than 4,700 ancient human genomes has now identified the possible origins of Celtic1 and Germanic2 languages and found migrations that might have dispersed their speakers around Europe — partly explaining their distribution today. The papers were published in Nature on 4 November.

Linguistic and archaeological studies have indicated that Celtic languages were widespread across Europe about 2,500 years ago, reaching into present-day Italy, Spain and France. Speakers of early Germanic languages might have been limited to a pocket of northern Germany, Scandinavia and the Baltic Sea coast some 3,000 years ago.

“We wanted to kind of see how this change occurs. How does the range swap through time?” says Hugh McColl, a population geneticist at the University of Copenhagen and a co-author of both studies.

How one language family took over the world: ancient DNA traces its spread

How one language family took over the world: ancient DNA traces its spread

Linguists have previously proposed that migrations played some part in the dispersal of Germanic and Celtic languages. But Guus Kroonen, a historical linguist at Leiden University in the Netherlands and a co-author of both studies, says that there are other ways for languages to spread. “You can easily adopt a new language without changing your genes.”

McColl, Kroonen and their colleagues looked for signs of migration through shifts in the ancestry of ancient population groups. To do so, they used newly sequenced genomes from more than 700 people, alongside published data from some 4,000 ancient humans.

The researchers identified an enigmatic population that migrated to Sweden around 4,000 years ago, possibly from Baltic regions. They found that the presence of this ancestry in Scandinavia and its spread throughout Europe was consistent with previous linguistic theories and archaeological evidence. “It’s a good tracer dye for the spread of Germanic languages,” says Kroonen.

For instance, the ancestry was present in southern Scandinavia and northern Germany around 3,000 years ago, when linguistic evidence points to exchanges with other language groups in this region. After some 1,000 years, the population moved into central, southern and western Europe, including the British Isles, which also chimes with linguists’ ideas and historical evidence about the spread of these languages, such as the first appearance of Germanic language inscriptions, called runes, around 2,000 years ago. The ancestry was present in Anglo-Saxon individuals in Britain, who spoke a Germanic precursor to Old English.

The study on the spread of Germanic languages also turned up a surprising ‘back-migration’ of people from present-day Germany into Scandinavia, which coincided with the emergence of Old Norse — the predecessor of modern Scandinavian languages — and with the Vikings’ influence on the region.

The Rök Stone, which bears the longest runic carving on stone with more than 700 characters, is thought to have been erected by Vikings in present-day Östergötland, Sweden.Credit: JEPPE GUSTAFSSON/TT News Agency/AFP via Getty

In many cases, the expansion of Germanic languages occurred in regions where Celtic languages were dominant.

Linguists debate both where Celtic languages emerged and how they became so widespread, says McColl, with some favouring an Atlantic origin overlapping with the current range of Celtic speakers in the British Isles. Other models put Celtic origins farther east, in Europe.

#1387. Stephen Robinson was just the latest Aberdeen manager to crash and burn... it's time to look at the club and its structure

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:30 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 17:30 EST, 9 November 2026

Across the space of two days last week, Aberdeen fans were dragged down memory lane only to emerge bruised and battered for their troubles.

Friday marked the 40th anniversary of plain old Alex Ferguson’s departure to Manchester United. It was an occasion for newspapers and TV bulletins to again recall the mind-blowing feats which led to the biggest club in Britain beating a path to Pittodrie.

Three Scottish championships, four Scottish Cups, a League Cup, the Cup Winners’ Cup and the Super Cup. The redrawing of the landscape of Scottish football.

There was something especially brutal about how those glories were juxtaposed beside the struggles of the soon-to-be former Dons boss, Stephen Robinson, 24 hours later.

After eight months of grim toil in the Granite City, the four-goal home thrashing the Northern Irishman suffered at the hands of Hibernian on Saturday blew away any lingering hope he retained of turning an increasingly desperate situation around.

A proven manager who was always simply the wrong fit for Aberdeen, Robinson will lick his wounds and come again.

Stephen Robinson is a proven manager who was always the wrong fit  for Aberdeen

But while a failure to live up to Fergie’s impossibly high standards might have done for those in Robinson’s shoes in the years which immediately followed the great man’s move to Old Trafford, no Aberdeen supporter in their right mind views things through that prism these days.

The majority of those who watched Saturday’s capitulation weren’t even born when Fergie’s Reds were running rampage throughout Europe.

They appreciate that the slayings of Real Madrid and Bayern Munich which they watched on YouTube were the highlights of a golden era for the club. One they know is not coming back.

In 2026, the expectation is more modest and hardly unreasonable. That with the fifth-highest average crowd in the country, Aberdeen should be in the top six almost every year, frequently playing in Europe most seasons and winning the odd cup. Yet, they’re miles off that right now.

While Jimmy Thelin did deliver a day in the sun by beating Celtic in the Scottish Cup final last year, that success was an anomaly. There have been just two top-six finishes in the past five years, with two ninth-placed finishes and one in tenth spot.

Given all that, it’s difficult not to recall the old wisdom about being careful what you wished for.

In Derek McInnes’ eight seasons at the club between 2013 and 2021, the team never finished below fourth and were runners-up four years on the spin. The League Cup was also secured in 2014.

A run of consistency and success which supporters had long craved was soon forgotten. McInnes’ familiarity and loyalty were eventually held against him.

Five managers later, Aberdeen appear to be as far away from reclaiming their status as one of the Scottish game’s powerhouses as they’ve ever been.

‘I think we’ve been waiting on it for four or five years,’ said Gothenburg legend Alex McLeish.

‘There’s been some signs, obviously winning the cup that year. You think that’s a wee springboard for the coming season and then it’s all kind of middle of the league, lower end of the league.’

As Robinson cleared his desk last night, even those fans who didn’t want him at the club in the first place would have been reluctant to hold him entirely responsible for the current ills.

The Northern Irishman is demonstrably a good manager. He guided St Mirren to three top-six finishes and the League Cup.

Thelin performed wonders across a long period at Elfsborg. Two years ago, he had Aberdeen sitting on top of the table.

Jim Goodwin was humiliated at Darvel, but now has buoyant Dundee United believing again.

Even Stephen Glass, a left-field choice to succeed McInnes, went on to enjoy success with Memphis 901 and as assistant to Robbie Keane at Ferencvaros.

When a club appoints one manager who doesn’t work out, it’s logical to question the individual. If five managers crash and burn, it says more about the environment and the structure they work in.

‘What is the solution?’ asked McLeish. ‘It’s definitely always down to what kind of players you’ve got.

Jimmy Thelin lifted the Scottish Cup before his Aberdeen career ended in disappointment

‘It’s trying to get a team to function together. To have forwards that you know can score, to have midfielders that can show a bit of quality, beat a man, playing one-twos, being accurate with your passing. Every bit of quality comes into it.

‘The manager will always get the worse side of it, you know, because they can’t sack 20 players.’

While it’s too late to save Robinson, the club do appear to have moved to address this particular shortcoming.

Back in March, Darren Mowbray returned to Pittodrie as head of recruitment three years on from his first stint which saw the captures of Bojan Miovski and Ylber Ramadani.

The trouble is that the mish-mash of players who were recruited by Jordan Miles, Chris Badlan and Nuno de Almeida are plainly not good enough.

Mowbray, it must be said, didn’t get too much right in the summer, either.

It’s not just the failure to sign players with the requisite pedigree and character which dismays the Aberdeen supporters.

When it was clear that Thelin’s time was up in January, the Swede was shown the door without there being a replacement waiting in the wings.

While there were legitimate reasons why Eirik Horneland couldn’t commit at that moment, the Dons’ hierarchy needed a Plan B.

Sandro Schwarz came to the Granite City for talks but nothing materialised, with Peter Leven remaining in interim charge.

With the pressure growing, Robinson – a wholly unpopular choice – was unveiled nine weeks and four days on. None of this reflected well on anyone involved.

Lutz Pfannenstiel, the sporting director, has written a book on his adventures in the game which included his recollections of the time he kept a penguin in his bath.

As Aberdeen’s hopes for the season have gone down the plughole, he’s not uttered a syllable in public.

Sporting director Lutz Pfannenstiel has had nothing to say during Aberdeen's recent troubles

With former FA bigwig Adrian Bevington now in the chief executive’s role, Pfannenstiel’s input into the recruitment of the new manager will be interesting.

And what role does Dave Cormack have to play? No one doubts the chairman’s passion for the club or his financial commitment to it.

But after seven years in the post, Pittodrie, on his watch, has acquired the unfortunate reputation of being a place where managers crash and burn. And you begin to suspect they might not be the sum total of the issues.

‘Dave Cormack is a close friend and I know he’s done everything in his power to try and get the Dons to a level,’ said McLeish. ‘We saw that Scottish Cup final victory a couple of seasons ago, but the league positions are not what Aberdeen fans expect.

‘Dave will be agonising. You know what it’s like if you get something wrong. You can’t sleep at night.

‘Dave will have been through all that kind of rigmarole as well. There’ll be a big burden on him right now.

‘He’s been stoic and he’s stood by the club. He has to have massive credit for that. It’s just about getting Aberdeen to cement their name back at the higher echelons of Scottish football.’

Alex McLeish was speaking at the announcement of William Hill as official sponsor of Walking Football Scotland. To find your nearest game visit walkingfootballscotland.org

#1386. Journey to Wembley: Halifax set sights on winning more fans and climbing mountain to the Football League as their FA Cup adventure is ended by route-one Cheltenham

By IAN HERBERT AT EV CHARGER POINTS STADIUM

Published: 21:00 EST, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 18:05 EST, 9 November 2026

The FC Halifax manager John McGrath’s father-in-law is the top British mountaineer Alan Hinkes OBE and he knows that he has something of a summit of his own to scale, as he walks straight from the team bus to the pitch, set in the lee of Cheltenham’s mist-shrouded Cleeve Hill.

McGrath is all-too familiar with this setting. He brought his Buxton team here in the FA Cup's second round last season and was on the fringes of a major upset – 2-1 up at half-time – before watching the game fall away.

Cheltenham are a much stronger club, 12 months on, but our few weeks with McGrath, an Irishman who 25 years ago was playing for Aston Villa against Liverpool in the Premier League, reveal his ambition for the National League side he joined this summer.

We’re alongside him and FC Halifax on our journey to Wembley, told through all 13 rounds, following a club as far as they go and then picking up with the team who knock them out, all the way to the final.

A mist-veiled evening at Halifax’s Shay Stadium, a few weeks back, revealed much about 46-year-old McGrath. He arrives with his two-man coaching team for a Q&A with fans who, when the evening’s proceedings are finished, form a long and orderly queue to talk to him, one-on-one. The team’s four-hour drive to Southend awaits the following morning. But McGrath has no eye for the clock.

This managerial journey is one he hadn’t anticipated when, aged 32, a serious foot injury ended his long career with Burton Albion. He secured a master’s degree in broadcasting and media at Staffordshire University and had begun spots for Sky Sports and BBC local radio, yet here he is on ‘the grass’ he'd never wanted to leave.

His wife Fiona is Director of Public Realm at Islington Council and their time together is some weeks limited to a coffee at Doncaster station, near their home, when he drops her before daybreak. ‘It’s our little half an hour,’ he relates. ‘We’re ships that pass in the night.'

Cheltenham edged out FC Halifax 2-0 in front of 2,961 fans to reach round two

Cheltenham boss Steve Cotterill shakes hands with Halifax manager John McGrath

Ground staff put up the goalposts at EV Charger Points Stadium, also known as Whaddon Road

His club’s fans are partisan – 350 are here – and yearn for League Two, though there’s not a fortune at McGrath’s disposal. The club’s owner David Bosomworth was at the club when it went bust in 2008 and they say that experience left him painfully aware of the need for sustainability. Fair enough. Bosomworth has declined to speak to us. He is not at Cheltenham.

An hour out from kick-off, McGrath is handing out training vests for the warm-up as well as observing things – it’s a modest backroom team – and that defeat last season perhaps plays on his mind. ‘Cheltenham tweaked it that day and personally, I think I should have done the same,’ he says. ‘I’m a better manager, 12 months on.’

The club could badly use the £50,000 prize money that a win here would bring, not to mention the accompanying shot of exhilaration.

McGrath already belongs in the margins of the tournament’s history. He and his son, Jay, a Doncaster Rovers player, became the first father and son to play in the same team in an FA Cup game when McGrath, Mickleover Sports' player-manager for their preliminary-round win against Coventry Sphinx in 2019, fielded his 17-year-old boy.

Halifax seem up for this challenge. Their players go looking for their kit in their bus's luggage compartment before the driver has jumped out to produce the key. But Cheltenham have come a long way in the past year.

The former Burnley owner Mike Garlick bought the club 15 months ago and his investment strategy has echoes of the methods which made the Turf Moor club a Premier League side for seven out of eight years. Manager Steve Cotterill, quickly installed by Garlick, was briefly with him at Burnley.

Cheltenham fans arrive at the ground with their side riding high, fifth in League Two

Halifax fans cheer on their side but their Cup run is over - they travel to Kidderminster next Saturday in the National League

Mike Garlick bought Cheltenham last year and quickly installed Cotterill as manager

There’s an air of optimism around the place, as head groundsman Paul Gibson attends to some stray grass cuttings with a leaf blower and husband and wife team Gerry and Hannah Oldham sort the kit.

The ground staff, with their distinctive West Country burr, take enjoyment from several attempts at installing the goalposts before getting them upright. Mascot ‘Whaddney the Robin’ is limbering up for a leisurely lap of the stadium.

Garlick suggests we use Cotterill’s office as a quiet place to talk as the stadium begins to fill up. He tries calling the manager for his consent to do so but Cotterill’s phone rings out in the room.

It turns out Cotterill is receiving calls on his watch. This is a source of some humour as Cotterill eventually barrels into the office, exhibiting his usual energy. The two men clearly get on.

Extra preliminary round, August 8: Nelson 3-2 Stockport Georgians

Preliminary round, August 22: Witton Albion 1-0 Nelson

1st qualifying round, September 5: Avro 0-2 Witton Albion

2nd qualifying round, September 19: South Shields 7-0 Witton Albion

3rd qualifying round, October 3: Buxton 0-2 South Shields

4th qualifying round, October 17: Halifax 3-2 South Shields

1st round, November 7: Cheltenham Town 2-0 Halifax

Garlick looks more at home here than at Burnley. He also owns Spanish third-tier side Antequera CF and a club in Gibraltar but yearned for this kind of environment and Cheltenham, tumbling towards the EFL exit last year, badly needed help.

‘I missed English football,’ Garlick says. ‘I thought this was a club where I could make a difference and have some impact. When I came in, we had four points from nine games and were bottom of the league. It was hard work last season, but the fans seem happy for me to be here.

'Everyone who comes up to me says “thanks for helping the club,” which is nice. I never quite got that at Burnley to be honest. I’ve probably got more thanks here in 12 months than in 17 years on the board at Burnley. But that’s football isn’t it?!’

There’s been substantial investment in the training ground, a new stadium hospitality lounge, and Cotterill’s contacts have contributed to some eye-catching signings including veteran former Villa forward Andreas Weimann from Rapid Vienna.

Halifax start the game well, with wingers Ben Tollitt and Connor Douglas both flying and Conor Carty, the Irish forward who has been a revelation this season, ready to receive. Twice, they go close in the early stages. But Cotterill has a very uncomplicated route-one method in place and whip-fast striker Kirsten Otchere, on loan from Leicester City, looks lethal.

Will Flint’s string of fine interventions for Halifax is matched by the excellence of goalkeeper True Grant but Otchere crosses from the left for Jake Evans to score, left-footed.

This time McGrath does change things, adjusting the defensive line to quell Otchere’s threat after half time. Cotterill, whose colourful touchline antics include shoving his full-back out of the way when he blocks his line of view, grows concerned as Cheltenham’s attacking threat fades and Halifax dominate.

Carty nets from a Douglas’ crosses but is offside. Halifax lack the moment of class to convert superiority into goals. Substitute George Miller’s late header ended Halifax’s tournament for another year.

Halifax's Ben Tollitt battles for possession but his side cannot find a way through Cheltenham

McGrath and his Halifax players applaud the travelling supporters after their Cup exit

The Cheltenham fans flood out into suburban Whaddon Road fortified in their belief that something is building. ‘An FA Cup run is great for morale and also a massive contribution to the finances, because we’re hopefully going to strengthen again in January and the summer,’ says Garlick.

A foggy trip up the M6 awaits Halifax, though McGrath brings both a hinterland and perspective to the quest of start filling the famous old Shay Stadium once more and pushing closer to the fourth tier after 24 years away. His father-in-law was the first Briton to climb all the world's 8,000m mountains, in the Himalayan and Karakoram ranges of Nepal, Tibet and Pakistan.

‘He’s one of the best in the world,’ McGrath relates. ‘And however tough it is being a footballer or football manager, you try sitting on the side of Mount Everest for three months.

‘There’s a rumour building in our town that we play good football, that there’s goals to be seen at our stadium and a bunch of talented young men are representing the club in the right way.

'We want to get another 800 fans a week through the door and kick the club up the division and into the Football League. We think we can do that.’

#1385. How a once-controversial idea is advancing understanding of Parkinson’s disease

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Rachel Nuwer is a freelance writer based in New York City.

Microbiologist Sarkis Mazmanian says environmental factors often have a role in Parkinson’s.Credit: California Institute of Technology

Myriam Penninckx was having lunch at a restaurant in Brussels when her right arm began to shake. This was just the latest in a string of signs that something might be amiss. Her handwriting had suddenly become impossible to decipher, and she had noticed herself slowing down, physically and mentally. “I had always been Speedy Gonzales, doing a lot of things at the same time,” she says. “But that was becoming less possible.”

Penninckx was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease shortly after her 60th birthday. She retired from her job and became depressed. “It was really hard to be someone who had a beautiful career, and then suddenly become a Parkinson’s patient,” she says. Her social life also ground to a halt. “If you have a tremor and you cannot cut your fish or eat your spaghetti, you don’t go out any more,” she says. “You close yourself to the world.”

When Penninckx heard about an unusual clinical trial being run at Ghent University in Belgium, she decided to enrol. In July 2021, she underwent a procedure that entailed flushing out her gut, and giving her a faecal transplant from a healthy donor to replace the community of microorganisms living there. The results, she says, “were amazing”. Her arm tremor went away and has not returned. She feels like the trial gave her “another shot at life”.

It might, at first, sound counterintuitive that such microbiome-targeting treatment could have marked benefits for people with Parkinson’s. Physicians have long been taught that the disease is a brain disorder that affects mainly the dopamine system, and that the hallmarks of the disease are Lewy bodies — misfolded clumps of a protein called α-synuclein that build up in neurons. But scientists have realized that the rest of the body is also involved, and the gut, in particular. For many individuals with Parkinson’s, evidence points to the gut’s involvement in the disease many years before diagnosis, says Per Borghammer, a neuroscientist at Aarhus University in Denmark.

Changes in the microbiome are also linked to some early symptoms and faster progression of the disease. These observations suggest that there are different subtypes of Parkinson’s, adds Filip Scheperjans, a neurologist at Helsinki University Hospital.

The gut’s seemingly central role in many Parkinson’s cases has implications not only for a better understanding of the disease’s origins and biology but also for tailoring treatments to an individual’s profile. “I make the comparison with what we see in oncology and cancer research,” says Arnout Bruggeman, the neurologist at Ghent University Hospital who oversaw Penninckx’s faecal transplant. Recognizing that various cancers exist as subtypes has allowed scientists to design vastly better treatments, he says — something he hopes will also be the case for Parkinson’s.

Hints that the gut is involved in Parkinson’s have been around since the disease was first described. People commonly have gastrointestinal issues, which sometimes start years before diagnosis. In 2003, researchers suggested that the α-synuclein pathology seen in the central nervous system might originate at peripheral sites, including the gut1. The work “introduced the idea that Parkinson’s disease starts very localized and then spreads via the neural connections”, Borghammer says. “It’s a little analogous to cancer that starts in one place and then metastasizes.”

Dozens of papers subsequently revealed that the microbiomes of people with Parkinson’s differ from those of people without the disease. In 2016, Sarkis Mazmanian, a microbiologist at the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena, showed that the microbiome plays a crucial part in the development of Parkinson’s-like symptoms in mice engineered to overexpress α-synuclein2. The animals’ symptoms went away when the researchers obliterated their microbiomes, and returned when they restored them. The team also transplanted human microbiomes into the mice, and found that rodents that received transplants from people with Parkinson’s had worse symptoms than did those who received transplants from healthy people.

In 2019, Borghammer and his colleague proposed that Parkinson’s can be divided into two main subtypes, according to where α-synuclein originates3. The ‘brain first’ subtype of the disease, he says, starts in the olfactory bulb, whereas a ‘body first’ version starts in the gut. This idea was controversial at first, and some researchers are still sceptical. But after years of mounting evidence, most are coming around to the idea.

Body-first Parkinson’s is thought to progress faster, and often manifests first with disturbances to the REM stage of sleep, gastrointestinal issues, depression, loss of smell and damage to the nerves that supply the heart (see ‘Teasing out distinct origins’). Brain-first Parkinson’s, by contrast, usually begins with motor symptoms. Eventually the subtypes converge — the end stage of the disease is the same, Borghammer says, it just starts in different places.

Source: P. Borghammer J. Neural Transm. 130, 737–753 (2023).

For both brain-first and body-first subtypes, the majority of Parkinson’s cases are attributable to “something you came across in your life”, Mazmanian says. Environmental risk factors seem to include air pollution, heavy metals, pesticides, certain viral infections and possibly microplastics.

Genes also play a part, however, and there is no bright-line distinction between genetic and environmental causes; the two are often linked. Variants of a gene called GBA1 are most closely associated with body-first Parkinson’s. But only a minority of carriers of the gene actually develop the disease, leading researchers to wonder what external factors might also have a role.

A study in April explored the part that the microbiome might play in increasing that risk, by examining hundreds of participants in the United Kingdom and Italy who did and did not have Parkinson’s, and likewise did and did not have a GBA1 variant linked to the disease4. The researchers analysed the participants’ stool samples and confirmed that the microbiomes of people with Parkinson’s differed significantly from those of people without the disease, and that the more severe the participant’s disease, the more altered was their microbiome. Mirroring earlier findings in mice, they also confirmed that, regardless of whether they carried a variant, people with Parkinson’s had roughly the same altered microbiome. This suggests that the disease process does more to transform a gut microbiome than do a person’s genes, says Elisa Menozzi, a clinical neuroscientist now at Aarhus University, and a co-author of the study.

As they had expected, Menozzi and her colleagues also found that healthy people carrying a GBA1 variant had, on average, microbiomes shifted toward the Parkinson’s pattern. But given that both carriers and non-carriers who already had Parkinson’s had statistically indistinguishable microbiomes, it seems that the variant itself is not what drives this change. Furthermore, in healthy participants not every carrier had this microbiome shift, and carriers who showed early, subtle signs of disease had microbiomes that looked most like those of people with Parkinson’s. Roughly one in five healthy participants without the variant also had the same altered microbiomes and signs that could be early markers of disease. The researchers’ interpretation, Menozzi says, is that changes to the microbiome raise the risk of Parkinson’s independently of genetics.

Taken together, Menozzi says, the findings suggest that the microbiome could be a diagnostic marker of Parkinson’s before symptoms become noticeable. Confirming this will require following the participants over time to see whether any of them develop Parkinson’s — something the team is doing, says co-author Anthony Schapira, a neurologist at University College London.

Although the study did not address what is causing the microbiome to change, the researchers found a significant association with participants’ eating habits. Diets that were high in vegetables, fruits and polyunsaturated fats seemed to protect against a Parkinson’s-type microbiome, whereas those high in saturated fat and low in fibre were associated with a microbiome closer to that of someone with the disease-altered microbiome. So dietary intervention is worth investigating, Schapira says. “The first question to answer is, can you do anything about this — can you change the microbiome?” he says. “ The next question is, does it matter?”

Some evidence from human trials already indicates that harnessing the microbiome to treat Parkinson’s could be possible. When Penninckx told her family that she would be receiving a faecal transplant as part of a study, she encountered some scepticism. “My grandchildren said, ‘Are you going to eat it?’” she recalls. She was relieved that was not the case. Instead, the researchers inserted a plastic tube into her nose, snaking it through her stomach and into her small intestine. “You’re never in contact with the material, so it’s not like there is a bad smell or taste,” she says.

Penninckx was one of 22 participants in the 2024 study to receive a faecal transplant from a healthy donor, while another 24 people were given a placebo made up of their own gut flora5. Twelve months after treatment, those who received the active treatment had fewer motor symptoms and less constipation than did those in the control group. The researchers plan to launch a larger trial this autumn to replicate these findings, Bruggeman says. Future trials will also analyse the composition of the microbiomes of healthy donors, which he says is “a key question” for determining the source of a potential positive effect.

Per Borghammer proposed that Parkinson’s can be divided into subtypes.Credit: Tonny Foghmar

Not all the results have been this promising. Scheperjans and his colleagues did not see a significant improvement in 30 participants who received an active treatment in a double-blind, placebo-controlled faecal transplant trial6. They do not know why their results differed from those in Belgium, but they suspect it might have had something to do with the method of delivery. The team administered treatment into the colon of participants rather than into the small intestine, which contains more immune cells than the large intestine. “It may be that for immune-system regulation, the small bowel is more important,” he says.

Surprisingly, the placebo group in this trial experienced more benefits than did the active treatment group. Up to 12 months after treatment, those in the placebo group had less constipation and more relief of some motor symptoms, as well as more changes to their microbiomes. The researchers think that this might be related to the bowel cleansing that all participants underwent before treatment — a hypothesis that they plan to test in a follow-up study. “If you have an abnormal microbiome, maybe the bowel cleansing gives you an opportunity to get recolonized with more normal bacteria,” Scheperjans says. “We’ll know if that’s the case after the next trial.”

Borghammer suspects that the differing faecal transplant results might come down to how “incredibly crude” the trials so far have been, simply because the field is so new. For example, researchers do not yet have the knowledge that would allow them to select the best donors for participants. Given this, he does not think that inconclusive results should be discouraging. “It’s plausible that it can work,” he says. “We just don’t understand it well enough yet.”

Another potential problem for faecal-transplant trials — and for research on Parkinson’s interventions in general — is that studies usually lump together people with body-first and brain-first subtypes. This could be confounding the results, Borghammer says, because different forms of the disease are likely to be driven by different mechanistic pathways. In 2022, for example, a phase III trial of an immunotherapy treatment targeting α-synuclein failed to produce significant results. But when the researchers later analysed the data for participants only with the most severe Parkinson’s, they found that the treatment did seem to slow progression of motor symptoms7. “It looks like for the fast-progressing type, which is strongly associated with the body-first type, it might have actually worked,” Borghammer says. “But because the original study included a mixed group of unselected patients, the clinical trial might have been unable to show statistically significant results.”

Myriam Penninckx was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease shortly after turning 60.Credit: Courtesy of Myriam Penninckx

Researchers are increasingly aware of these limitations, and some groups are looking more closely at the bacterial species and mechanisms involved — and at more targeted populations. Haydeh Payami, a geneticist at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, and her team found that the gut microbiomes of about one-quarter of people with Parkinson’s contain high levels of a protein that induces aggregation of α-synuclein8. That protein is produced only by the bacterium Escherichia coli, giving scientists “one defined target”, says Mazmanian, who collaborates with Payami. Vertero Therapeutics, a firm Mazmanian co-founded in Woburn, Massachusetts, have developed a drug that inhibits production of the E. coli protein, and in mice it prevented α-synuclein from aggregating. “You can just stop this process in its tracks,” Mazmanian says.

In May, Vertero began a phase I trial in people with Parkinson’s whose microbiome matches the bacterial profile targeted by the drug. “In the population that we can treat, our hope is to slow down or even stop Parkinson’s progression,” Mazmanian says. “That would be a huge victory.”

The ultimate goal, however, is to be able to identify people in the very early stages of the disease, and then use pharmaceuticals, faecal transplants, dietary changes or other interventions to alter their trajectory. “Fast forward a decade, I hope we’ll be able to treat people before they actually develop Parkinson’s,” Mazmanian says.

Five years on, Penninckx still feels empowered by the gains she experienced in the faecal-transplant trial. She keeps busy as a board member of Parkili, a Belgian charity that supports scientific research — including some of Bruggeman’s work — and arranges trips around the world for people with Parkinson’s. She has travelled to Jordan with the group, and in May, she and seven others represented it at the World Parkinson’s Conference in Phoenix, Arizona. “I’ve started a new life,” she says. “So my story is a happy one.”

Penninckx knows that her disease is not cured. But her experience hints at the potential benefits that the mounting appreciation of the Parkinson’s gut–brain connection could bring.

#1384. Steely Chelsea triumph despite losing Martinez to head injury

This was the afternoon when Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea went from swashbuckling to stoic, thrilling to tenacious.

For all Alonso’s attacking vigour at the start of his reign, there can have been no more symbolically satisfying victory under the new coach than this resolute win at Everton – the most vivid example of an increasingly impressive transformation.

This was what Alonso described as “winning in a different way”. A triumph amid the adversity of losing goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez to what appears to be a serious injury after a head collision with Jarrad Branthwaite is just one facet of why the joyous visiting supporters might consider this an early turning point.

Where recently they wilted, on Saturday they thrived in securing a first Premier League clean sheet for nine months.

Much more of this and the adjectives which were splattered across Chelsea during the golden years of José Mourinho – solid, robust and dogged – will be part of the Stamford Bridge lexicon once more.

“Just one day,” Alonso warned, both acclaiming the importance of the win while wisely preaching caution. “It will be key when we manage 10 clean sheets, even though this one feels good. We need to repeat it again and again, but the mentality was very good. Sometimes it is not to play nice, it is to play good – to win second balls, and to be efficient. We needed one of these: a clean sheet and a win.”

Asked about Martinez’s condition, Alonso said: “It was a concussion, but beyond that I do not know. I have only seen one clip of the incident, so we need to wait.

“What we know is that he left the stadium conscious and is now in hospital undergoing precautionary tests.

“We need to wait. Hopefully it will not be too serious, but at the moment we just have to wait.”

Alonso is speedily shifting perceptions of this previously underperforming bunch, the Stamford Bridge culture on and off the pitch already unrecognisable from a few months ago.

It was Chelsea’s trip to Everton last season which facilitated the endgame of Liam Rosenior’s short, but generally hideous reign.

For those who tried to banish memories, it was a darkly comical period when Chelsea’s players were paying their respect to stationary footballs, seemingly finding new ways to stand in front of travelling fans to apologise for meek and rancid performances.

How different the scenes after Pedro Neto’s double on Merseyside – a success built on those old-fashioned and too often underestimated qualities of character and application before the artists had the final say. These are the wins that build connections and trust between players and supporters, especially during the getting-to-know-you period of a managerial tenure. While neutrals mutter about a generally disappointing spectacle, the players and supporters return home clutching three points believing they have fought together in the trenches.

Neto fires past Pickford to double Chelsea's lead! 🔥 Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/SOJeBP5mq0

It cannot be overlooked how this win owed a debt to the erratic refereeing of Paul Tierney, especially the amnesty he offered to Morgan Rogers on the stroke of half-time.

Already booked, Rogers was fortunate not to receive a second caution for a lunge on James Garner which took the man after the ball. A replica challenge by Everton’s Harrison Armstrong had warranted a yellow card in Tierney’s world just 21 minutes earlier.

The home team’s argument that this was a potential game changer was supported when the England midfielder was inevitably involved in the move which led to Neto breaking through 44 seconds into the second half – a lead Chelsea never looked like surrendering as Everton’s attacking limitations were exposed.

Chelsea break the deadlock inside a minute of the second half! ⚡ Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/E63rtGQnbv

That should not disguise how this is a different Chelsea, contrasting not just with the characterless and rudderless team of last season, but also the defensively flawed version that began this one. Mike Penders deputised for the stricken Martínez – conscious but taken to hospital as a precaution – and was well-protected.

As much as Alonso’s artistry as a midfield maestro is presumed to define him as a coach, one cannot help but believe there are many who underestimate him as a football student. He was never going to return to England clinging to one idea given his previous Premier League experience, and he intuitively knew an away game at Everton was one for foot soldiers.

He signed Jordan Henderson for such a task. Just like his manager, the former Liverpool captain was primed for enemy territory.

Alonso’s anticipation of a fixture in which a battle had to be fought before there was an outbreak of football proved correct, aided by the fussy and generally terrible first-half officiating of Tierney.

Bizarrely, Alonso had as much cause to curse Tierney for the first of several contentious decisions, booking Armstrong for an aggressive but ultimately fair lunging challenge on Josh Acheampong. That enraged the home supporters to inspire Everton to their most dangerous spell, Thierno Barry coming closest to troubling Martínez before half-time.

Although Moisés Caicedo was denied a goal-of-the-season contender when a vicious 20-yard volley struck the crossbar, the scrappy, stop-start flavour of the occasion initially suited the hosts.

Caicedo rattles the woodwork with a stunning effort! 💥 Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/CSIM9ogtSp

Rogers’s reprieve changed all that. Inexplicably inconsistent as Tierney was, Chelsea exhibited a steel which thrilled Alonso as much as those games when Cole Palmer, Rogers and João Pedro are in full flow.

“They didn’t score, but did a fantastic job for the team,” Alonso pointedly said of his attackers.

Alonso’s name has not echoed so loudly across the Mersey since he played a few miles down the road from Everton’s new home. After several calamitous appointments, those fans can believe their team are in safe hands again.

A good win for Chelsea at Everton, but above all, let’s hope Martinez is back to full health soon.

Moyes accepted that his side had were not good enough.

He told TNT Sports: “We were a little bit unlucky with the goals. It wasn’t good defending, but it takes a couple of deflections before it gets to Neto. It makes it a relatively easy finish for him.

“The second one was a free-kick which obviously ricochets around, so I think there were parts of the game we did OK, but we didn’t offer enough to create enough, to make enough chances. I can’t think of many, so that is probably the biggest indictment.”

He had a minor gripe over a first-half tackle that was reviewed, saying, “I think the Morgan Rogers tackle on Jimmy [Garner] could have been questioned.”

However, given the good start to the season for Everton so far, he does not have too much rancour.

"Not as good as we wanted." 💬 David Moyes reflects on Everton's defeat to Chelsea 🔵 🎙️ @jules_breach | Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/qPU64VjHYC

Speaking to TNT Sports after the match, Xabi Alonso gives relatively positive news on Emi Martinez.

He describes the planned tests as “precautionary” and says, “as far as I know, he left the stadium conscious.”

Neto added more detail to his thoughts on the game.

On his first goal, he explained how Everton’s defensive approach allowed them to react: “We know that they came man-to man. In the second half we adjusted some stuff. We tried to get the best of the man-to-man press and we got away. We got the cross and I could finish well, so really happy.”

He credited his Portugal coach, Jorge Jesus, with his calmness in front of goal, adding: “This comes a little bit from the new coach of the national team that says when you are near to the area you need to pass to the goal, so really happy with that.”

With Chelsea now in the Champions League places, Neto was keen to keep up the momentum. He said: “It’s really important. We know it’s tough to play away, even at home there are no easy games. We came here with personality, with good intentions to win the match and really happy with the result.”

You can follow all the 3pm games here with our clockwatch.

Leading the charge for your attention is Brentford, who welcome Liverpool.

In a quick post-match interview with TNT Sports, Chelsea forward Pedro Neto says “this win is for him” after Martinez’s grim injury.

He said: “A shame for Emi but we wish him all the best … this win is for him. A clean sheet in his honour. In the second half we adjusted some stuff.”

Xabi Alonso leads the celebrations as Chelsea salute the away end! 🥳 Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/AfwQAdYAmu

Everton are now in sixth place, but they might drop further. Their are five teams beneath them who would leapfrog them with a win, and Liverpool, Hull and Leeds amongst them are just a point behind.

Three points for Chelsea, who move into fourth place and keep their first Premier League clean sheet in nine months. Everton were enthusiastic, but they were ragged and then fell away once they went behind.

Chelsea, meanwhile, started loosely but tightened up, and became increasingly efficient.

However, both sets of players will likely be looking to follow up with Emi Martinez after he was forced off after a clash of heads with Jarrard Branthwaite, and was set to go to hospital. Let’s hope we get some good news soon over his health.

Quenda is on for Neto, who is likely the matchwinner.

Everton are focusing on long balls now. It’s not edifying, and so far it’s not effective either.

Chelsea’s last Premier League clean sheet was on January 17th, nine months ago.

There are nine minutes or so still to come from the added time indicated, but we may get more because of that late goal, and these two substitutions.

⬅️ Caicedo, Hato ➡️ Lavia, Palestra 🍬 0-2 ⚪️ [90] #CFC | #EVECHE https://t.co/Xq7zvjyXEB

Palmer smashes the ball into the wall from the free-kick, and the ball drops into the box.

Neto is the fastest to react, and he calmly slots the ball home off his left. Two clever finishes for the player today.

Neto fires past Pickford to double Chelsea's lead! 🔥 Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/SOJeBP5mq0

Penders drops the ball as he tries to claim a long throw. It is worked back to Barry to head towards goal, and Penders deals with that far more calmly. Palestra and Welbeck are set to come on for Chelsea. Norgaard is the latest booking, dragging Palmer’s shirt as hard as he can. Eight yellows so far.

The free kick is about 25 yards out and well placed for Palmer, in the middle of the goal.

It’s three on one for Chelsea’s frontline. Tarkowski is the one man, holding them up as he covers both balls for Palmer. He opts for Pedro to his right, but he fires far too close to Pickford. That should have been game over, but Chelsea wasted a golden chance.

Penders races from the edge of the six-yard box to punch clear from just inside the area.

Grealish and Armstrong are replaced by Christian Norgaard - making his debut since his move from Arsenal - and Johnson.

A quick update on Martinez. The goalkeeper has been taken to hospital for further checks and treatment. That is all the detail we have for now.

Tarkowski appears to catch Rogers in the box as he turns towards goal, but the video review gives nothing.

It’s a corner on the left wing for Chelsea. Henderson takes, but it’s cleared, and Palmer’s shot from 30 yards is well struck, but wide.

Brennan Johnson will be on soon, it seems, as Moyes starts chasin’ it.

10 minutes of normal time remaining, and Everton are playing almost as if they’re holding on, but they’re behind.

Chelsea have already scored THREE goals in the opening minute of a Premier League half this season ⚡️ They've only played seven games. https://t.co/4ZSJR7cekd

Chelsea’s defeat in this stadium last year was the nadir of the Liam Rosenior era - a symbol of everything wrong with a team devoid of spirit and character. If they take three points from here, overcoming the setback of losing their keeper in such a manner, it will be a symbol of rapid transformation under Alonso. One would expect Everton to test rookie Premier League keeper Mike Penders in the last 25 minutes, although they’ve shown little threat since going behind.

Martinez is applauded off the pitch by both sets of fans. That will mean we’ve got about 10 minutes of added time to come.

Penders replaces him. Branthwaite is still playing.

Martinez cannot continue due to injury and is replaced by Penders for his #PL debut. 🍬 0-1 ⚪️ [74] #CFC | #EVECHE https://t.co/knGUEB0iGH

Martinez is now being moved onto the stretcher next to him. They are not rushing this, and that is the most important thing for now. It’s always an odd atmosphere in a match when something like this happens, for the players who stay on.

The TNT commentators note that Martinez is moving his arms, so we can hope that is a positive sign.

Mike Penders is being readied to come on.

He’s thought of very highly at the club, and could be a future No. 1 with the club, but clearly the focus is on Martinez’s health for now.

It is of course close to the anniversary of Petr Cech’s head injury at Reading, in 2006.

The stretcher is ready for Martinez, but he continues to get treatment on the pitch.

Medical staff rush onto the pitch to check their players over.

Branthwaite gets to his feet, but Martinez is still down. It was a really big contact for both men.

William Estevao has, apparently, played just 44 minutes for Xabi Alonso this season.

Given the relatively poor performance of the Chelsea frontline today, might he make an appearance?

A rapid second-half start. 🔥 #CFC | #EVECHE

Grealish twists and turns into space on the left. He stands up a cross that, at full strength, Martinez claims despite the glare of the sun.

The game has reverted to its scrappy feeling, which now suits Chelsea better, for a change.

Ainsley Maitland-Niles comes off, with former Chelsea players Tyrique George on in his place.

Merlin Rohl does brilliantly to clear a cross which looked to be a real threat.

Meanwhile, Everton have not posted since this, perhaps taken aback by the start.

HT. Goalless at the break. [0-0] #EVECHE https://t.co/seo2ZKOfhZ

It was inevitable Rogers would be involved in Chelsea’s opening goal given he is fortunate to still be on the pitch. Shall we write up Moyes’ post-match remarks now? He will be livid.

Armstrong clears an Acheampong cross for a corner. Neto will take, swinging it in. Pickford beats it away.

Rogers and Hato combined so well in the build-up. That combination was fairly quiet in the first half, so this may be a shift of focus from Alonso for the second period.

The away side get in front. Rogers holds up the ball well, rolls the ball forward for Hato’s run. He clips the ball inside that runs to Neto, who controls with one touch, and clips in an accurate finish 44 seconds into the half.

Chelsea break the deadlock inside a minute of the second half! ⚡ Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/E63rtGQnbv

Martinez, the Chelsea goalkeeper, is treated to the sunlight in his eyes.

Xabi Alonso will perhaps be concerned that his team have looked relatively toothless so far. They have recoiled from the match at times, though continued to create a few chances.

David Moyes will likely know that all this will mean nothing if they can’t convert Chelsea’s frayed temper into a scoreline advantage.

I think it’s fair to say that Chris Bascombe has seen enough of this ref.

Today’s second ‘game is gone’ moment of the afternoon is the camera scanning to Chelsea’s set-piece coach Austin McPhee after Caicedo was denied a goal of the season contender, crashing Henderson’s corner against the crossbar with a stunning volley.

“So Moises I’ve a cunning plan for you to do a Marco van Basten impression, but from an extra 15 yards out…”

Meanwhile, the questions of how Morgan Rogers is still on the pitch after his challenge on Garner will dominate the half-time chat.

Referee Tierney has been atrocious and we all need a break from him.

An eventful match without too many chances.

Jordan Pickford and Emi Martinez have both been alert to danger, but the match is mainly fraying at the edges. Fouls and tempers are the story, with a subtext of bookings creeping up.

Armstrong clears a flick-on off the line for the third corner.  Chelsea put the pressure on, but Everton clear for now.

Pickford pushes a Neto shot over the bar. Mykolenko nodes behind for another corner at the near post, and then again for the next set piece.

The Chelsea players continue to complain. Garner needs to go off as he received treatment, but Rogers remains on.

A poor clearance from Martinez puts Chelsea in trouble, but Rogers closes him down to put it out of play. Armstrong goes down. Moments later, Rogers and Garner go in hard on a 50-50, and there is yet more complaining from the players. Both players’ studs connected with the other, it seems.

This could go south for one or both of them, depending on how the ref sees it, but the check clears them both.

Chelsea captain Reece James’ surgery could be out for a couple of months, Xabi Alonso explained.

He told the  press: “I wish him the best recovery. We won’t set timelines, but we expect him to be out for several weeks. It’s not going to be short. Whether it’s before or after Christmas then time will tell. It needs to be done properly.”

He is looking to vice captains Moises Caceido and Levi Colwill to step up in his absence, explaining: “You can be a captain without an armband, for sure. Leadership is important and that’s why we have this group, not just on matchday.”

James remains vital to Chelsea at their best, and while his minutes have been managed, it’s a huge disappointment to see him need to go under the knife once more.

In his press conference ahead of the weekend, Everton boss David Moyes was not too concerned by his relatively small squad.He said:  “Leicester City won the league with not too many players. We have not got too many players. I am not saying we’re going to win the league, but we want to try to challenge and be around the top teams.”

That might be made harder by the news that the Friedkin Group are already looking to sell the club after only a couple of years in charge. Moyes is a rare thing, a manager who keeps improving despite setbacks, and his second spell has been fairly solid so far.

Moyes is aware that Chelsea pose a threat up front, adding: “Their attacking line is incredibly exciting. I also think they have got some super defenders as well, but they are playing quite an expansive game, which on its day can lead to goals and on another day it can lead to defeats.”

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Everton vs Chelsea.

Chelsea return to Premier League action this weekend looking to harness the momentum of their emphatic 5-1 victory over Bournemouth before the international break. That Stamford Bridge masterclass ended a frustrating three-match winless streak and was built upon braces from Joao Pedro and Jordan Henderson, alongside another strike from summer signing Morgan Rogers.

Yet the true catalyst for the resurgence was the return of Moises Caicedo. Having shaken off the calf problem that hindered his early-season involvement, the midfielder anchored the side’s win. While defensive vulnerabilities persist - extending an unwanted run of league matches without a clean sheet back to January - the victory offered clear signs of progress under their head coach, Xabi Alonso.

Next up is a notoriously difficult trip to Merseyside to face Everton in Saturday’s lunchtime fixture. Historically, Everton have proven to be a formidable stumbling block for the capital club, particularly on home turf. Everton enter the weekend unbeaten in eight of their last nine home encounters against Chelsea, a stretch that has seen the Londoners fail to score on seven visits and suffer six defeats, including a chastening 3-0 reverse last term that spelt the end for Liam Rosenior.

David Moyes will demand a sharper defensive showing from his side this time around, following a frustrating 2-2 draw with Hull City where a 2-1 lead slipped away. Even so, Everton’s broader defensive record at home offers encouragement, having kept clean sheets in two of their opening three league fixtures at their base.

With both teams eager to build consistency, Saturday’s clash pits Chelsea’s newly found attacking spark against an opponent that traditionally relishes this fixture.

#1382. 'I've never revealed the whole story': England fans wouldn't boo me if they knew the truth, says Ben White... as he defends World Cup walkout and rejecting call-ups

Published: 15:00 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 18:20 EST, 9 November 2026

Ben White believes England fans would not boo him if they knew the truth behind his 2022 World Cup walkout.

The Arsenal defender left the camp in Qatar after the group stages citing 'personal reasons', although a fallout with Gareth Southgate's assistant, Steve Holland, was later reported. He then declined a return to the England set-up while Southgate and Holland were in charge but was included by Thomas Tuchel in March of this year.

However, White was booed by fans inside Wembley when he came on in the second-half of a friendly against Uruguay, only to score his first international goal and then concede a late penalty in a 1-1 draw. He was not selected for the World Cup in North America but is back with the squad ahead of this week's Nations League fixtures against Croatia and Spain.

And the 29-year-old, addressing those jeers for the first time, said: 'It was hard to hear, especially because they didn't know the situation, which is kind of what I put my mind to.

'They don't know my situation and it is not really about what I have done, because they don't know why, and if they did they would not be booing or saying these things. I just think about maybe (them) not knowing the full story, and if they did, maybe they wouldn't (boo).'

He added: 'Obviously, a load has been said. I've probably seen all of it. I just think people don't know the full story, because I've never said anything, and I won't put anyone under the bus or share any of that.

Ben White has insisted he would not be booed by England fans if they knew the truth behind his World Cup walkout

White fell out with former England assistant Steve Holland (left) before heading home during the 2022 World Cup

'There were loads of things that happened and communication wasn't great. I don't want to throw anyone under the bus. A lot of people try to do that to me so it's something I wouldn't want to do myself. I think it's probably the best way. It's a bit tricky and not straightforward, but it's amazing to be here now. It's a privilege to be called up.'

White, however, is adamant that he would make the same decision today and leave the World Cup, even if he will not divulge the reasons as to why.

'I don't think I would (do anything different),' he said. 'I think, as a person, I'm quite real, and I made the decision that I would probably continue to make. It's one that I'm not happy about. It wasn't ideal. But it happened, it's time to move on.

'I don't think I am looking to win anyone over or say anything that helps them get back on my side. It is what it is. There are reasons for it and I am just looking forward to playing for England and doing well and looking for success.'

White has spoken publicly about not watching football, and this, too, has been used against him by some supporters.

'It doesn't mean I don't like football, because I do it every day, so I must like it a little bit!' he said. 'It's because I don't watch it, which I think is quite normal for someone that does a job and then doesn't go home and then continue watching that job.

'I don't think anyone knows my personality. I keep that to my loved ones and family. It's all noise when people have an opinion on that stuff. It is not actually me. People don't know me and I like it that way. You give so much to the game, which is intense. I think it's important to keep some bits for yourself. I keep the energy for the people I love.'

England new boy Josh King believes his aptitude for academia gives him an advantage at the start of a burgeoning career.

The Fulham star – who has two Premier League goals this season – linked up with Thomas Tuchel’s squad on Monday morning as one of two fresh call ups alongside Jobe Bellingham.

King was a straight-A student at the renowned independent Hampton School in south London, with alumni including Queen guitarist Sir Brian May and golf pro Paul Casey.

The teenager’s mother, Michelle, is a university lecturer and finishing a PhD on sickle cell disease while his father Steve is a personal injury lawyer.

‘The most important thing about being good academically and education-wise is you’re able to take on information much more quickly,’ King said.

‘You can take on information which might take a bit longer for other people. I think that definitely helps.’

While the 19-year-old was invited to take part in a pre-World Cup training camp in Miami, he is hoping to make his international bow against Croatia on Thursday.

Although a central figure in Fulham’s midfield, a confident King could be utilised wider by Tuchel were he to be given an opportunity across the two-game Nations League camp.

‘There was a buzz around Fulham when I got called up [this week],’ he added. ‘I got off the phone with the boss, ran into the kitchen and started cheering with my dad. I called mum at work and she was screaming in the office. This felt slightly unachievable when I was younger.’

Jude Bellingham and Harry Kane were namechecked as those who helped him settle when introduced to the group in Florida, with King having also studied the likes of Jamal Musiala and Pedri to elevate his own game.

‘The main thing you take is the standards they set,’ he said when reflecting on joining the camp in America. ‘The way they conduct themselves, the way they perform every day, the way they train and the way they take everything seriously.

‘The little things, technical things, the way some people strike the ball, the way some people pass, just little things which you almost take without thinking about it - they also have an impact.

‘On a few occasions I asked “how do you finish this way” or “what do you do in this scenario” and it always helps to add to my game.’

#1380. ‘Historic change’: what the 2026 US mid-term election results mean for science

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Paediatrician Annie Andrews, a Democrat, won a US Senate seat in South Carolina in a surprise victory on 3 November. Democrats had not won a Senate seat in the state since 1998.Credit: Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty

The US mid-term elections swept the Democratic party to power in both chambers of the US Congress, raising hopes that lawmakers will now push back against disruptions to science introduced by the administration of Republican President Donald Trump.

The results will mark the end of nearly two years in which the Republicans controlled the presidency and both congressional chambers — and many scientists around the world are celebrating the change as an opportunity to protect the country’s research system.

How the US mid-term elections could shake up science

How the US mid-term elections could shake up science

“This is a big win,” says Megan Peters, a cognitive scientist who moved in 2025 from the University of California, Irvine, to University College London, in part because of worries about US science. “It’s a demonstration that US [voters] are dissatisfied with what the current administration has been doing.” Scientific research, she adds, “is America’s superpower, and it’s been cut at the knees”.

Those hopeful for change include researchers affected by the US Agency for International Development (USAID) being shut down early in Trump’s presidency. “I’m cautiously optimistic,” says Quarraisha Abdool Karim, an epidemiologist at the Centre for the AIDS Programme of Research in South Africa, which is headquartered in Durban and had partnered with USAID on clinical trials. “What we’ve seen in the past 24 hours is that democracy and democratic principles, with individuals turning out to vote, can make a huge difference.” But, she adds, “we will not see overnight changes”.

As of 2.15 p.m. EST on 4 November, Democrats had secured at least 237 seats in the 435-seat US House of Representatives and 54 seats in the 100-member US Senate, giving them decisive majorities in both, with votes still being counted in some states. These majorities will give them the power to craft legislation that counteracts Trump’s science agenda, although there will still be obstacles. For instance, given that Democrats haven’t won two-thirds of the seats in both chambers of Congress, the president can veto those bills.

Trump initially told The New York Times that he would accept the mid-term election results and that he would “look forward” to working with Democrats. Later, however, he posted an image of a red hat with the word ‘VETO’ on it to Truth Social, his social-media platform.

Since Donald Trump became president for the second time in January 2025, his administration has pushed for unprecedented cuts to science funding, politicized decision-making at federal science agencies and interfered with policies at US universities that receive federal funding.

When Democrats take charge of both chambers of the US Congress on 3 January 2027, they will be able to control congressional committees, including science committees; set agendas for hearings that investigate government officials and their science policies; and use legally binding subpoenas to compel the Trump administration to provide documents and testify in front of Congress.

‘Science needs defending’: record number of researchers run for office in US mid-terms

‘Science needs defending’: record number of researchers run for office in US mid-terms

On social media, Democrats promised to make use of that authority. Robert Garcia, a representative from California who will soon chair the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, shared a two-word statement aimed at the Trump administration: “Lawyer up.” In particular, some scientists are calling for scrutiny of Russell Vought, director of the White House Office of Management and Budget, who has drafted a plan that gives political appointees, rather than scientist peer reviewers, control of decisions about research grants, and who has delayed the distribution of congressionally approved science funds.

Scientists and policy specialists said they were hoping to see more congressional oversight of the actions of Robert F. Kennedy Jr, the head of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), who has questioned vaccine safety, and whose tenure has coincided with the country’s worst measles resurgence in decades. “For sure, secretary Kennedy will be put on the hot seat” to explain his unscientific actions, says Georges Benjamin, executive director of the American Public Health Association in Washington DC. “What I’m hoping is that Congress will really push this administration to have a much more proactive response to the measles epidemic.”

Zoe Lofgren, a Democratic representative from California, said she would campaign to become the head of the House Science, Space and Technology Committee, which oversees agencies such as NASA and the US National Science Foundation. “We will hold this administration accountable for the damage they have done to the American scientific enterprise,” she said in a statement.

Stand Up for Science, a science-advocacy group based in Atlanta, Georgia, that has organized protests against the Trump administration’s reshaping of US science, says that it will release a plan on 5 November with strategies to push Congress for change.

Whether Congress will be able to increase funding for federal science, rather than just hold it relatively steady as they have for the past two years, is doubtful, however. Susan Collins, a Republican senator from Maine and chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, had protected science budgets, but she lost her re-election bid in these mid-terms. Large boosts to science spending could also just be difficult to pass, given that the budget must also be signed by Trump, who has tried to slash non-defence science spending.
